title: Raymond Cattell, Hans Eysenck, the Five-Factor Theory, HEXACO, and the Dark Triad
overview: This chapter presents the trait, or genetics, approach to personality. Raymond Cattell used factor analysis on huge amounts of data from normal people to find the basic structural units of personality, which he called traits. He classified traits in several ways (common vs unique; ability, temperament and dynamic; surface vs source; constitutional vs environmental-mold), identified 16 source traits measured by the 16 PF Questionnaire, estimated that about one-third of personality is inherited, described six life-span stages, and gathered L-data, Q-data and T-data, favouring the multivariate approach with its R and P techniques over bivariate and clinical methods. Hans Eysenck reduced personality to three inherited superfactors: extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, linked to cortical arousal and nervous-system reactivity and supported by twin, adoption and cross-cultural research. Robert McCrae and Paul Costa's five-factor model (neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness), measured by the NEO Personality Inventory, has been found across more than 50 nations, is fairly stable across the life span and predicts a vast range of emotional and behavioural outcomes. Michael Ashton and Kibeom Lee's HEXACO model adds an honesty/humility factor, and Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams' Dark Triad describes narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy. The chapter ends with research on traits and Internet behaviour and a reflection that heredity may account for up to half of personality, though environment cannot be discounted.
objectives: Explain Cattell's goal of predicting behaviour and how factor analysis was used to identify traits.
Distinguish Cattell's ways of classifying traits: common/unique; ability, temperament and dynamic; surface/source; constitutional/environmental-mold.
Describe Cattell's 16 source traits and the 16 PF Questionnaire, including its uses, variations and research findings.
Outline Cattell's six stages of personality development and identify the Freudian ideas he incorporated.
Compare Cattell's L-data, Q-data and T-data, and his bivariate, clinical and multivariate (R and P technique) research approaches.
Evaluate Cattell's theory, including criticisms of subjectivity in factor analysis and his standing as father of the trait approach.
Define behavioral genetics and summarise the evidence for genetic influences on personality.
Describe Eysenck's three dimensions (E, N, P), their biological bases and the twin, adoption and cross-cultural evidence for their heritability.
Explain McCrae and Costa's five-factor model, the NEO-PI, and research on its heritability, cross-cultural consistency, gender differences and stability over time.
Summarise the emotional and behavioural correlates of the Big Five, including well-being, success, health, addiction, crime and relationships.
Describe the HEXACO six-factor model and how it differs from the five-factor model.
Identify the Dark Triad traits, how they are assessed, and their behavioural correlates.
Discuss how personality traits relate to Internet and social media behaviour, and evaluate the trait approach as a whole.

sections.heading: Predicting Behavior
sections.detailed:
The chapter opens with Cattell's own definition: personality is whatever allows us to predict what a person will do in a particular situation. This sets the tone for the whole trait approach, whose aim is prediction rather than cure.

Goal: prediction, not therapy. Cattell wanted to forecast how someone would respond to a given stimulus situation. Unlike the clinically oriented theorists who came before him (who built their theories on case studies of unhappy or disturbed patients seeking change), Cattell had no interest in turning abnormal behaviour into normal behaviour. His subjects were normal people, and his aim was to study their personality, not to treat it. He argued that it is impossible, or at least unwise, to try to change a personality before fully understanding what is to be changed.

A scientific approach. Cattell's method was rigorously scientific, relying on observed behaviour and very large amounts of data. It was common for him to take more than 50 different measurements from a single subject. Horn (2001) judged that no other theory matched his for comprehensiveness and reliance on empirical evidence.

Factor analysis. The hallmark of Cattell's work was the way he treated his data. He used factor analysis, a statistical technique that examines the correlation between every possible pair of measures taken from a group of people in order to find common underlying factors. For example, scores on two tests, or on two subscales of one test, are correlated. If two measures correlate highly, Cattell concluded that they tap the same or a related aspect of personality. For instance, if anxiety and introversion scales correlated highly, both could be taken as measuring one personality characteristic. The two sets of data are then combined into a single dimension or factor.

Personality traits. Cattell called these factors traits and defined them as the mental elements of personality. Only by knowing a person's traits can we predict how that person will act in a given situation. To understand someone fully, we must therefore describe precisely the whole pattern of traits that makes that person an individual.
sections.simple: Cattell wanted to predict what people would do, not to cure them, so he studied normal people rather than patients. He collected huge amounts of data and used factor analysis, a statistical method that groups together measures that correlate highly. Each group, or factor, is a trait, and knowing someone's traits lets us predict their behaviour.
keyPoints: Cattell defined personality as what permits prediction of behaviour in a given situation.
He studied normal people to understand personality, not to treat or change it.
His approach was rigorously empirical, often with 50+ measures per subject.
Factor analysis correlates pairs of measures; highly correlated measures are combined into one factor.
Factors are traits, the mental elements of personality, needed for prediction.

sections.heading: The Life of Cattell (1905–1998)
sections.detailed:
An older brother and wounded soldiers. Cattell was born in Staffordshire, England. His parents set high, demanding standards of behaviour but let the children spend their free time as they pleased; he and his brothers and friends sailed, swam, explored caves and fought mock battles. At age 9, when England entered World War I, a nearby mansion became a hospital and he watched trainloads of wounded soldiers arrive from France. He said this made him unusually serious and aware that life is short and one must achieve while one can, which may explain his lifelong intense dedication to work. He also felt strongly competitive with an older brother whom he could not overcome, and wrote about the struggle to keep his own freedom of development.

Psychology: a bad choice. At 16 he entered the University of London to study physics and chemistry, graduating with honours in three years. London deepened his interest in social problems, and he realised the physical sciences could not address social ills, so he decided to study the human mind. This was a brave choice in 1924: psychology in England offered few jobs, only six professorships in the whole country, and was seen as a field for eccentrics. Against friends' advice he did graduate work at London with Charles E. Spearman, the psychologist-statistician who developed factor analysis. Whereas Spearman used factor analysis to measure mental abilities, Cattell resolved to apply it to the structure of personality.

A time of hardship. After his Ph.D. in 1929 he found his friends had been right: there were very few jobs. He lectured at Exeter University, wrote a book on the English countryside and set up a school psychology clinic in Leicester while continuing research. Overwork, poor diet and a cold basement flat gave him chronic digestive problems, and his wife left him because of his poor prospects and total absorption in work. Yet he felt this period made him focus on practical problems rather than theory, and made him canny, ascetic and impatient with irrelevance.

Success in America. Eight years after his doctorate, Edward L. Thorndike invited him to spend a year at his Columbia University laboratory. Cattell then took a professorship at Clark University, and in 1941 moved to Harvard, where his colleagues included Gordon Allport and William Sheldon (who was developing his body-type theory). He married a mathematician who shared his research interests and at 40 settled at the University of Illinois as a research professor. He produced more than 500 articles and 43 books, working every day without distinction (he once arrived at an empty lab on Thanksgiving). In his 70s he joined the University of Hawaii, still working as hard as a young professor seeking tenure. He died in Honolulu at 92, a year after receiving the American Psychological Association's Gold Medal Award for Life Achievement, honouring among other things his factor-analytic mapping of personality.
sections.simple: Cattell grew up in England, and seeing wounded World War I soldiers as a boy made him serious and driven. He studied chemistry, then switched to psychology under Spearman, the inventor of factor analysis, and decided to apply it to personality. After years of poverty and hardship he found success in the United States, producing over 500 articles and 43 books.
keyPoints: Born in Staffordshire, England; wounded WWI soldiers and rivalry with an older brother shaped his dedication to work.
Studied physics and chemistry, then psychology under Charles Spearman, who developed factor analysis.
Applied factor analysis to personality rather than to mental abilities as Spearman had.
Years of hardship after his 1929 Ph.D. made him practical and ascetic.
Worked with Thorndike, then at Clark, Harvard, Illinois and Hawaii; 500+ articles, 43 books; APA Gold Medal before his death at 92.

sections.heading: Cattell's Approach to Personality Traits: Common, Unique, Ability, Temperament, Dynamic, Surface and Source Traits
sections.detailed:
Cattell defined traits as relatively permanent reaction tendencies that form the basic structural units of personality. He classified them in several ways (summarised in Table 8.1).

Common traits and unique traits. A common trait is one that everyone possesses to some degree, such as intelligence, extraversion and gregariousness. Everyone has them, but in different amounts. Cattell argued that common traits are universal because all people share a similar hereditary potential and face similar social pressures, at least within one culture. People also differ because of unique traits, aspects of personality shared by few others. Unique traits show up especially in interests and attitudes: one person may be absorbed by genealogy, another by Civil War battles, baseball or Chinese martial arts.

Ability, temperament and dynamic traits. A second classification divides traits by what they do. Ability traits determine how efficiently we can work toward a goal; intelligence is an example, since our level of intelligence affects how we pursue goals. Temperament traits describe the general style and emotional tone of behaviour, such as how assertive, easygoing or irritable we are; they affect how we act and react to situations. Dynamic traits are the driving forces of behaviour, defining our motivations, interests and ambitions.

Surface traits and source traits. A third classification is based on stability and permanence. Surface traits are characteristics that correlate with one another but do not form a factor, because they are not determined by a single source. For example, anxiety, indecision and irrational fear combine to form the surface trait Cattell labelled neuroticism, which therefore has no single source. Because surface traits are composed of several elements, they are less stable and permanent and so less important for describing personality; Table 8.1 adds that they may weaken or strengthen in different situations. Source traits are more important: they are unitary, much more stable and permanent personality factors. Each gives rise to some aspect of behaviour, and source traits are the individual factors, derived from factor analysis, that combine to account for surface traits.

Table 8.1 thus lists eight kinds of traits: common, unique, ability, temperament, dynamic, surface, source, plus the constitutional and environmental-mold subtypes of source traits discussed next.
sections.simple: Cattell saw traits as fairly permanent tendencies to react in certain ways. Some traits everyone has in some amount (common), while others belong to only a few people (unique). Traits can also be about ability, emotional style (temperament) or motivation (dynamic). Surface traits are clusters of behaviours with no single source, while source traits are stable, single factors underneath them.
keyPoints: Traits are relatively permanent reaction tendencies, the basic structural units of personality.
Common traits are shared by all in varying degrees; unique traits belong to one or a few people (seen in interests and attitudes).
Ability traits = efficiency toward goals; temperament traits = emotional style; dynamic traits = motivation.
Surface traits correlate but have no single source (e.g. neuroticism from anxiety, indecision, irrational fear) and are less stable.
Source traits are unitary, stable, permanent factors that combine to produce surface traits.

sections.heading: Constitutional Traits and Environmental-Mold Traits
sections.detailed:
Cattell classified source traits by their origin into two types.

Constitutional traits arise from biological or physiological conditions, but they are not necessarily innate. The chapter's example is the use of alcohol or drugs, which can produce behaviours such as carelessness, talkativeness and slurred speech. The point is that the source is bodily, even if it is not inherited.

Environmental-mold traits come from influences in our social and physical environments. They are learned characteristics and behaviours that impose a pattern on the personality. A person raised in a poor inner-city neighbourhood is shaped differently from one raised in upper-class luxury, and a career military officer shows a different behavioural pattern from a jazz musician. Table 8.1 gives examples such as behaviour shaped by friends, work environment or neighbourhood.

Why it matters. By recognising both kinds of source traits, Cattell acknowledged the interaction between personal (biological) and situational (environmental) variables. This links forward to his work on heredity and environment and to his position on the nature-nurture issue in the Questions about Human Nature section, where the chapter describes constitutional traits as innate and environmental-mold traits as learned.

Exam note. Review Question 5 asks about the difference between source traits and environmental-mold traits; since environmental-mold traits are themselves a type of source trait, the useful contrast is between the two origins of source traits: constitutional (biological) and environmental-mold (learned).
sections.simple: Source traits can come from two places. Constitutional traits come from the body or biology (for example, behaviour caused by alcohol), though they are not always inherited. Environmental-mold traits are learned from our social and physical surroundings, like the different habits of a soldier and a jazz musician.
keyPoints: Source traits are classified by origin as constitutional or environmental-mold.
Constitutional traits originate in biological conditions but are not necessarily innate (e.g. effects of alcohol or drugs).
Environmental-mold traits are learned from social and physical environments (e.g. neighbourhood, occupation).
The distinction shows Cattell recognised interaction between personal and situational variables.

sections.heading: Source Traits: The Basic Factors of Personality
sections.detailed:
After more than twenty years of intensive factor-analytic research, Cattell (1965) identified 16 source traits as the basic factors of personality. They are best known through the objective test that measures them, the Sixteen Personality Factor (16 PF) Questionnaire. Each factor is a bipolar dimension with a low and a high pole (Table 8.2):

A: reserved, aloof, detached vs outgoing, warmhearted, easygoing.
B: low vs high intelligence.
C: low ego strength, easily upset, less emotionally stable vs high ego strength, calm, emotionally stable.
E: submissive, obedient, docile, meek vs dominant, assertive, forceful.
F: serious, sober, depressed, worrying vs happy-go-lucky, enthusiastic, cheerful.
G: expedient, low in superego vs conscientious, high in superego.
H: timid, shy, restrained vs bold, adventurous.
I: tough-minded, self-reliant vs tender-minded, sensitive, dependent.
L: trusting, understanding, accepting vs suspicious, jealous, withdrawn.
M: practical, down-to-earth, detail-focused vs imaginative, absentminded.
N: forthright, naive, unpretentious vs shrewd, worldly, insightful.
O: self-assured, secure, complacent vs apprehensive, insecure, self-reproaching.
Q1: conservative, traditional, dislikes change vs radical, liberal, experimenting.
Q2: group-dependent, joins and follows others vs self-sufficient, resourceful, independent.
Q3: uncontrolled, lax, impulsive vs controlled, compulsive, exacting.
Q4: relaxed, tranquil, composed vs tense, driven, fretful.

The chapter notes that these factors are described in ordinary everyday words we use about our friends and ourselves, so readers can easily guess where they stand on each.

Additional temperament traits. Cattell later identified further factors, which he called temperament traits because they concern the general style and emotional tone of behaviour. Examples are excitability, zest, self-discipline, politeness and self-assurance (Cattell, 1973; Cattell & Kline, 1977).

Source traits as atoms. In Cattell's system, source traits are the basic elements of personality in the same way that atoms are the basic units of the physical world. He argued that psychologists cannot understand personality or formulate laws about it without precisely describing these elements.
sections.simple: Through decades of factor analysis, Cattell found 16 source traits, such as reserved vs outgoing, serious vs happy-go-lucky, and relaxed vs tense. They are measured by the 16 PF Questionnaire. He later added more temperament traits like zest and politeness, and he saw source traits as the 'atoms' of personality.
keyPoints: Cattell (1965) identified 16 source traits after 20+ years of factor analysis.
They are measured by the Sixteen Personality Factor (16 PF) Questionnaire.
Each is bipolar: factors A, B, C, E, F, G, H, I, L, M, N, O, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4.
Later temperament traits added: excitability, zest, self-discipline, politeness, self-assurance.
Source traits are the basic elements of personality, like atoms in physics.

sections.heading: Dynamic Traits: The Motivating Forces
sections.detailed:
Cattell described dynamic traits as those concerned with motivation, an issue central to many personality theories. Earlier in the chapter (p. 217) dynamic traits are defined as the driving forces of behaviour that set our motivations, interests and ambitions, and Table 8.1 describes them as the forces underlying our motivations.

Cattell's key argument was that a theory of personality which ignores dynamic, or motivating, forces is incomplete. He used an analogy: it is like describing an engine but never mentioning the kind of fuel it runs on. Ability traits tell us how efficiently a person can work toward a goal and temperament traits tell us the emotional style of the behaviour, but dynamic traits explain why the person is moving at all.

Place in the system. Dynamic traits form one third of Cattell's second classification (ability, temperament and dynamic traits). Together with source traits, they show that Cattell aimed at a complete account: what the units of personality are (source traits), how they are styled (temperament), how well they work (ability), and what drives them (dynamic traits).

Note on coverage. This edition of the chapter gives only this brief treatment of dynamic traits. It does not describe subtypes of dynamic traits (such as ergs, sentiments or attitudes) or define the self-sentiment, even though Review Question 8 asks about self-sentiment; students should consult a fuller source on Cattell for that question.
sections.simple: Dynamic traits are the motivating forces behind behaviour: our drives, interests and ambitions. Cattell said a personality theory without motivation is like describing an engine but forgetting to mention its fuel.
keyPoints: Dynamic traits concern motivation: the driving forces behind behaviour, interests and ambitions.
Cattell held that a theory ignoring motivation is incomplete.
Analogy: describing an engine without mentioning its fuel.
Dynamic traits complete the ability-temperament-dynamic classification.

sections.heading: The Influences of Heredity and Environment
sections.detailed:
Cattell was very interested in how much heredity and environment each contribute to personality.

Method. He compared, statistically, the degree of similarity found between four kinds of pairs: twins reared in the same family, twins reared apart, non-twin siblings reared in the same family, and non-twin siblings reared apart. By comparing how alike these pairs were, he could estimate how far differences in traits were due to genetic rather than environmental influences. Pairs who share more genes (twins) and pairs who share an environment (reared together) give different combinations of genetic and environmental overlap, which is what makes the comparison informative.

Findings. For some traits heredity plays a major role. Cattell's data suggested that about 80 percent of intelligence (Factor B) and 80 percent of timidity versus boldness (Factor H) could be attributed to genetic factors.

Overall conclusion. Across all traits, Cattell concluded that about one-third of personality is genetically based and two-thirds is determined by social and environmental influences.

Significance. This made Cattell, along with Allport, one of the first to argue that inherited factors shape personality and rank in importance with environment (p. 226). His later research on 16 PF data (Cattell, 1982) went further, identifying specific source traits that were primarily inherited (F, I, Q3) and others primarily environmental (E, G, Q4), covered in the research findings section. The chapter's later theorists, especially Eysenck, place even more weight on heredity.
sections.simple: Cattell compared twins and ordinary siblings, raised together or apart, to estimate how much of each trait is inherited. He found that some traits, like intelligence (B) and boldness (H), are about 80 percent genetic. Overall he concluded that one-third of personality is inherited and two-thirds comes from the environment.
keyPoints: Compared twins and non-twin siblings, each reared together or apart.
Estimated the share of trait differences due to genes vs environment.
About 80% of intelligence (Factor B) and of timidity vs boldness (Factor H) attributed to genetics.
Overall: one-third of personality genetic, two-thirds social/environmental.

sections.heading: Stages of Personality Development
sections.detailed:
Cattell proposed six stages of personality development covering the whole life span (Table 8.3).

Infancy (birth to 6). This is the major formative period. The child is influenced by parents and siblings and by weaning and toilet training. Social attitudes develop, together with the ego and superego, feelings of security or insecurity, attitudes toward authority and a possible tendency toward neuroticism. Although Cattell was not a Freudian, he borrowed several Freudian ideas here: that the early years are crucial in forming personality, and that oral and anal conflicts can affect personality.

Childhood (6 to 14). This stage has few psychological problems. It marks the beginning of a move toward independence from parents and increasing identification with peers.

Adolescence (14 to 23). This is a more troublesome and stressful period. Emotional disorders and delinquency may appear as young people experience conflicts centred on drives for independence, self-assertion and sex.

Maturity (23 to 50). Generally a productive and satisfying time regarding career, marriage and family. Personality becomes less flexible than before, so emotional stability increases. Cattell found little change in interests and attitudes in this period.

Late maturity (50 to 65). Personality develops in response to physical, social and psychological changes. Health, vigour and physical attractiveness may decline and the end of life may come into view. People re-examine their values and search for a new self, often after their children have left home. The chapter notes this resembles Carl Jung's view of the midlife period.

Old age (65 onward). This stage involves adjusting to many kinds of loss: the death of a spouse, relatives and friends; loss of career through retirement; loss of status in a culture that worships youth; and a pervasive sense of loneliness and insecurity.

Evaluation points. Cattell's scheme is notable for covering the entire life span rather than stopping in childhood, for combining Freudian emphasis on early experience with later-life change similar to Jung, and for linking personality change to concrete life circumstances.
sections.simple: Cattell described six life stages: infancy (0-6, the key formative period), childhood (6-14, calm and peer-focused), adolescence (14-23, stressful), maturity (23-50, settled and stable), late maturity (50-65, re-examining values) and old age (65+, coping with losses). He borrowed Freud's idea that early years and oral and anal conflicts matter.
keyPoints: Infancy (0-6): major formative period; weaning, toilet training, ego, superego and social attitudes form.
Freudian borrowings: importance of early years and of oral and anal conflicts.
Childhood (6-14): few problems, move toward independence and peers; Adolescence (14-23): conflicts over independence, self-assertion and sex.
Maturity (23-50): productive, less flexible, more emotionally stable, little change in interests.
Late maturity (50-65): re-examining values, similar to Jung's midlife; Old age (65+): adjusting to losses, loneliness, insecurity.

sections.heading: Questions about Human Nature
sections.detailed:
Cattell's definition of personality as that which allows prediction of what a person will do reveals his view of human nature.

Free will vs determinism. For behaviour to be predictable, it must be lawful and orderly; prediction would be hard without regularity and consistency in personality. The chapter's example is a spouse who can predict accurately what the partner will do because the partner's past behaviour has been consistent. Cattell's view therefore allows little spontaneity, since spontaneity would make prediction harder, and he falls more on the side of determinism.

Ultimate goals. Cattell proposed no ultimate or necessary goal that dominates behaviour: no drive for self-actualisation pulling us toward the future and no psychosexual conflicts pushing us from the past.

Role of childhood. He recognised the impact of early life events but did not believe childhood forces determine personality permanently. This is a key contrast with Freud, for whom early psychosexual conflicts are decisive (useful for Review Question 7).

Nature vs nurture. Cattell accepted both. The chapter illustrates this with his source traits: constitutional traits are described as innate, whereas environmental-mold traits are learned.

Uniqueness vs universality. He took a moderate position, recognising common traits that apply to everyone in a culture and unique traits that describe the individual.

Optimism vs pessimism. His personal view is clearer. When young he was optimistic about humanity's ability to solve social problems; he expected greater awareness and control over the environment, rising intelligence and a more gracious community life of creatively occupied citizens. Reality did not meet his expectations, and he eventually came to believe that human nature and society had regressed.
sections.simple: Because Cattell wanted to predict behaviour, he assumed behaviour is orderly and consistent, so he leaned toward determinism. He saw no single life goal, and childhood mattered but did not fix personality forever. He accepted both heredity and environment, both common and unique traits, and grew from optimism to pessimism about society.
keyPoints: Prediction requires lawful, orderly behaviour, so Cattell leans toward determinism and allows little spontaneity.
No ultimate goal: no self-actualisation pull and no psychosexual push.
Early life matters but childhood does not permanently determine personality (unlike Freud).
Accepts both nature (constitutional) and nurture (environmental-mold); moderate on uniqueness vs universality.
Personally moved from youthful optimism to believing human nature and society had regressed.

sections.heading: Assessment in Cattell's Theory: L-data, Q-data and T-data
sections.detailed:
Cattell's objective measurement of personality relied on three main techniques, which he called L-data (life records), Q-data (questionnaires) and T-data (tests).

Life records (L-data). Observers rate specific behaviours that people show in real-life settings such as a classroom or an office. Examples include how often someone is absent from work, school grades, conscientiousness in performing job duties, emotional stability on the soccer field or sociability in the office. The key feature is that L-data involve overt behaviour visible to an observer, occurring in a natural setting rather than the artificial situation of a psychology laboratory.

Questionnaires (Q-data). Here people rate themselves rather than being rated by observers. The chapter summary adds that Q-data come from questionnaires, personality inventories and attitude scales. Cattell recognised two limitations. First, some people have only superficial self-awareness, so their answers will not reflect their real personality. Second, even people who know themselves well may not want the researcher to know them and may deliberately falsify their answers. He therefore warned that Q-data must not automatically be assumed accurate.

Personality tests (T-data). Cattell used what he called objective tests, in which the person responds without knowing which aspect of behaviour is being assessed. This gets round the weaknesses of Q-data: if you cannot guess what the researcher is looking for, you cannot distort your answers to hide your traits. For example, faced with an inkblot, you could not predict whether your response would be interpreted as showing you to be conservative, relaxed, adventurous or apprehensive. Cattell regarded the Rorschach, the Thematic Apperception Test and the word-association test as objective because they resist faking.

Criticism of the label. The chapter points out that most psychologists find this use of 'objective' misleading. These tests are usually called subjective, because biases affect how they are scored and interpreted. Cattell meant objective in the sense of hard to fake, not in the sense of free from scorer bias.
sections.simple: Cattell gathered three kinds of data. L-data are observers' ratings of real-life behaviour, like attendance or grades. Q-data are people's ratings of themselves on questionnaires, which can be inaccurate or faked. T-data come from tests like inkblots where people cannot tell what is being measured, so they are hard to fake, though most psychologists call such tests subjective.
keyPoints: L-data: observer ratings of overt behaviour in natural settings (absences, grades, sociability).
Q-data: self-ratings on questionnaires; limited by poor self-awareness and deliberate faking.
T-data: 'objective' tests where the person cannot tell what is measured, so they resist faking.
Cattell counted the Rorschach, TAT and word-association test as objective.
Most psychologists call these tests subjective because of scoring and interpretation biases.

sections.heading: The 16 PF (Personality Factor) Test
sections.detailed:
Of the several tests Cattell developed, the most notable is the 16 PF Test, built on the 16 major source traits.

Features. It is designed for people aged 16 and older and gives a score on each of the 16 scales. Responses are scored objectively, and computerised scoring and interpretation are available. It is widely used in research, clinical diagnosis and predicting job success, and has been translated into about 40 languages.

Reading a profile. Figure 8.1 shows a sample profile for a hypothetical airline pilot, plotted as percentile ranks between the low-score and high-score descriptions of each factor. Reading its high and low points, this person is emotionally stable, conscientious, adventurous, tough-minded, practical, self-assured, controlled and relaxed, and is not tense, apprehensive or timid. The example shows how a profile translates into a practical picture relevant to a job, which is why the test is used in personnel selection.

Variations. Cattell produced several versions. There are scales for specific aspects of personality such as anxiety, depression and neuroticism; versions for special purposes such as marriage counselling and evaluating the performance of business executives; and forms for children and for adolescents.

Research highlights. The chapter's research box (p. 225) summarises that the 16 PF can predict marital stability, can be faked by people wanting to look good, can be used in many cultures though literal translation is impossible in some languages, has shown that some source traits are mainly inherited and others mainly environmental, can identify 16 source traits, and can be used for research, clinical diagnosis and predicting job success.
sections.simple: The 16 PF Test measures Cattell's 16 source traits in people aged 16 and over. It is scored objectively, translated into about 40 languages, and used for research, clinical diagnosis and job selection. A profile, such as the sample airline pilot's, shows a person's high and low points on each trait, and special versions exist for children, teens, marriage counselling and executives.
keyPoints: Based on the 16 source traits; for ages 16+; yields 16 scale scores.
Objectively scored, with computerised scoring and interpretation; ~40 languages.
Used for research, clinical diagnosis and predicting job success.
Sample pilot profile: emotionally stable, conscientious, adventurous, tough-minded, practical, self-assured, controlled, relaxed.
Variations for anxiety, depression, neuroticism, marriage counselling, executives, children and adolescents.

sections.heading: Research on Cattell's Theory: Bivariate, Clinical and Multivariate Approaches
sections.detailed:
Cattell identified three ways of studying personality: the bivariate, clinical and multivariate approaches.

The bivariate approach. Bivariate means two-variable. This is the standard laboratory experiment: the psychologist manipulates an independent variable and observes its effect on the subjects' behaviour, the dependent variable. It is also called univariate because only one variable is studied at a time. Cattell granted that this method is scientific, rigorous and quantitative, but argued that it covers only limited aspects of personality. In reality personality is affected by many interacting variables, and in the artificial laboratory significant emotional experiences cannot be manipulated or reproduced. So for Cattell the bivariate approach was too restrictive to reveal much about traits.

The clinical approach. This includes case studies, dream analysis, free association and similar techniques. As noted in Chapters 2 and 5, these methods are highly subjective and do not produce verifiable, quantifiable data. Cattell quipped that the clinician has his heart in the right place but is a little fuzzy in his head (1959).

The multivariate approach. Cattell chose this approach because it yields highly specific data. It uses the sophisticated statistical procedure of factor analysis, and Cattell favoured two forms of it. The R technique collects large amounts of data from a group of people and correlates all the scores to identify personality factors or traits. The P technique collects a large amount of data from a single subject over a long period.

Why it matters. The contrast explains Cattell's whole programme: he rejected the narrow experiment and the vague clinic in favour of measuring many variables at once and letting factor analysis reveal the underlying structure. The R technique tells us about traits across people; the P technique tells us how traits are organised and vary within one individual over time.
sections.simple: Cattell named three research methods. The bivariate (lab experiment) method is rigorous but studies too little at once. The clinical method (case studies, dreams) is too subjective. He preferred the multivariate method using factor analysis: the R technique looks at lots of data from many people, and the P technique looks at lots of data from one person over a long time.
keyPoints: Bivariate (univariate) approach: manipulates one independent variable; rigorous but too restrictive for personality.
Clinical approach: case studies, dreams, free association; subjective and unquantifiable ('heart in the right place, fuzzy in his head').
Multivariate approach: factor analysis of many variables; Cattell's choice.
R technique: large data from a group, correlated to find traits.
P technique: large data from one subject over a long period.

sections.heading: A Sample of Research Findings
sections.detailed:
The chapter samples a few of the hundreds of factor-analytic studies by Cattell and his associates, plus later studies using his test.

Heredity vs environment of specific traits. A factor analysis of 16 PF data from 3,000 males aged 12 to 18 led Cattell (1982) to conclude that three source traits are determined mainly by heredity: Factor F (serious vs happy-go-lucky), Factor I (tough-minded vs tender-minded or sensitive) and Factor Q3 (uncontrolled vs controlled). Three others are determined mainly by environment: Factor E (submissive vs dominant), Factor G (expedient vs conscientious) and Factor Q4 (relaxed vs tense). This answers Review Question 6.

Marital stability. Cattell and Nesselroade (1967) gave the 16 PF to married couples classed as having stable or unstable marriages, the criterion being whether the couple had taken steps to end the marriage. Factor analysis showed that marital stability could be predicted from test scores: partners in stable marriages had similar personalities, while partners in unstable marriages had very different ones.

Faking. Like other personality tests, the 16 PF can be distorted. College students, prisoners and substance abusers took it twice, first honestly and then trying to present themselves favourably; the two sets of responses differed significantly (Simon, 2007).

Translation problems. In South Africa, translation into the Tshivenda language changed the meanings of items so much that responses were invalid; as with some other tests and languages, a literal translation was impossible (Van Eeden & Mantsha, 2007).

Successful translations. A satisfactorily translated Greek version clearly distinguished Greek elementary and preschool teachers from the norms for the general Greek population (Roussi-Vergou, Angelosopoulou, & Zafiropoulou, 2009; Roussi-Vergou & Zafiropoulou, 2011). A Turkish translation was also found to be a valid measure of personality differences (Aksu et al., 2010).

Taken together, the findings show the test's predictive power and cross-cultural use, along with its vulnerability to faking and translation difficulties.
sections.simple: Cattell found that traits F, I and Q3 are mostly inherited, while E, G and Q4 are mostly shaped by environment. The 16 PF predicted which marriages were stable (similar partners stayed together). But the test can be faked, and it did not work when translated into Tshivenda, though Greek and Turkish versions were valid.
keyPoints: Cattell (1982), 3,000 males aged 12-18: F, I, Q3 mainly hereditary; E, G, Q4 mainly environmental.
Cattell & Nesselroade (1967): similar partners in stable marriages, dissimilar in unstable ones.
Simon (2007): honest vs favourable answers differed significantly, so the 16 PF can be faked.
Van Eeden & Mantsha (2007): Tshivenda translation invalid; literal translation impossible.
Greek version distinguished teachers from national norms; Turkish version valid.

sections.heading: Reflections on Cattell's Theory
sections.detailed:
Criticism: subjectivity in factor analysis. Cattell rightly claimed factor analysis is objective and precise, but critics argue that subjectivity can creep in at several stages, because the researcher must make decisions influenced by personal preference. At the start, researchers decide which tests to use and which behaviours to measure. They then choose which factor-analytic technique to apply and what level of statistical significance to accept. Once factors are identified, the researcher must name them, and ambiguous labels may not accurately express what a factor is. The chapter stresses that this is not an inherent weakness in Cattell's theory but a potential for subjective error in the method. This subjectivity may explain why other researchers have had difficulty replicating Cattell's findings and confirming his 16 source traits.

Cattell's isolation. Cattell knew he had failed to persuade many psychologists, yet defended his approach as the only valuable one. At 85 he again criticised contemporary psychologists for not mastering and applying factor analysis and lamented that his work remained outside mainstream personality theory. He stayed convinced that his work would one day allow behaviour to be predicted as accurately as astronomers predict the movements of planets.

Positive evaluation. Current opinion among personality psychologists affirms the value of his approach. He is generally regarded as the father of the personality trait approach and one of the most influential psychologists of the 20th century (Denis, 2009; Revelle, 2009; Tucker, 2009). Whatever happens to his specific proposals, the trait approach and the investigation of genetic influences that he started continue to fascinate researchers, as the rest of the chapter shows.

For a 10-mark evaluation, strengths include rigorous empiricism, massive data, comprehensiveness, a widely used test (16 PF), life-span stages and early attention to heredity; weaknesses include subjectivity in data selection, technique and labelling, poor replication of the 16 factors, technical difficulty and isolation from the mainstream.
sections.simple: Critics say factor analysis is not fully objective, because researchers choose the tests, the techniques, the significance levels and the names of factors. This may be why others could not replicate his 16 traits. Even so, Cattell is seen as the father of the trait approach and one of the 20th century's most influential psychologists.
keyPoints: Subjectivity can enter factor analysis in choosing tests, techniques, significance levels and factor labels.
Others have struggled to replicate Cattell's 16 source traits.
Cattell saw his approach as the only valid one and lamented isolation from the mainstream.
He believed behaviour would one day be predicted as accurately as planetary movement.
Now regarded as father of the trait approach and among the most influential 20th-century psychologists.

sections.heading: Behavioral Genetics
sections.detailed:
The chapter has already noted growing evidence that some traits are influenced by heredity. The field that studies the connection between genetics and personality is often called behavioral genetics, defined in the margin as the study of the relationship between genetic or hereditary factors and personality traits.

The central claim is that, whatever method is used to evaluate or investigate personality, a significant genetic component must be taken into account. Allport and Cattell were among the first to propose that inherited factors shape personality and rank in importance alongside environmental factors.

This heading acts as a bridge in the chapter. Having shown Cattell's twin and sibling comparisons (about one-third of personality genetic) and his findings that some source traits are mainly inherited, the chapter turns to other researchers who pursued the causal link between genetic inheritance and personality: Hans Eysenck, whose three dimensions are said to be primarily inherited; McCrae and Costa, whose five factors are biologically based and largely heritable; and later models (HEXACO and the Dark Triad). The chapter's final reflection returns to behavioral genetics, noting that inheritance may account for as much as 50 percent of personality and that findings from behavioral genetics may require restructuring research that previously focused on early family and social interaction.

This is why the textbook groups these theorists under the genetics approach: each uses factor-analytic or trait-based measurement and emphasises the hereditary basis of the traits identified.
sections.simple: Behavioral genetics studies how genes and heredity relate to personality traits. The chapter says any study of personality must consider a significant genetic component. Allport and Cattell were among the first to say inherited factors matter as much as environment, and the rest of the chapter looks at researchers who followed that idea.
keyPoints: Behavioral genetics: study of the relationship between hereditary factors and personality traits.
A significant genetic component must be considered whatever method is used.
Allport and Cattell were among the first to rank inherited factors with environmental ones.
Bridges to Eysenck, McCrae and Costa and other genetics-oriented models.

sections.heading: Hans Eysenck (1916–1997)
sections.detailed:
Resigned to psychology. Hans Eysenck was born in Berlin and moved to England in 1934, after Hitler came to power in Germany. He wanted to study physics at the University of London but was told he lacked the necessary academic background. Discouraged, he asked whether there was any other science he could major in and was told there was always psychology. He had to ask what that was, was assured he would like it, and enrolled in a subject whose scientific status he later thought was more doubtful than his advisers realised. Over 40 years later, by then very successful, he was asked whether he regretted the choice; he said he often did, but was resigned to it.

A prolific record. Eysenck published 79 books, some for the general public, and 1,097 journal articles. At his death he was the world's most frequently cited psychologist (Farley, 2000). Unfortunately, after he died his wife destroyed all his personal and professional papers (Harris, 2011).

Assessment devices. He developed several instruments: the Eysenck Personality Inventory, the Eysenck Personality Profiler, the Maudsley Medical Questionnaire and the Maudsley Personality Inventory.

Contribution. His work was pivotal both in supporting the role of inheritance in personality and in integrating the scientific study of personality into psychology as a whole (Corr, 2007; Revelle & Oehlberg, 2008; Rose, 2010). He spent most of his career at the University of London's Maudsley Hospital and Institute of Psychiatry, researching the measurement of personality.
sections.simple: Eysenck was born in Berlin, fled to England in 1934, and ended up in psychology only because he could not study physics. He published 79 books and over 1,000 articles and was the world's most cited psychologist when he died. He created tests like the Eysenck Personality Inventory and helped make the study of personality more scientific and genetically based.
keyPoints: Born in Berlin; emigrated to England in 1934 after Hitler took power.
Took psychology only because he lacked the background for physics; said he often regretted it but was resigned.
79 books and 1,097 articles; most frequently cited psychologist at his death (Farley, 2000).
Developed the Eysenck Personality Inventory, Eysenck Personality Profiler, Maudsley Medical Questionnaire and Maudsley Personality Inventory.
Pivotal in supporting inheritance of personality and integrating personality into scientific psychology.

sections.heading: The Dimensions of Personality
sections.detailed:
Agreement and disagreement with Cattell. Working at the Maudsley Hospital and Institute of Psychiatry, Eysenck agreed with Cattell that personality consists of traits or factors derived by factor analysis. But he also criticised factor analysis and Cattell's research, because of potential subjectivity in the technique and difficulty replicating Cattell's results. So although he used factor analysis, he supplemented it with personality tests and experimental studies covering a wide range of variables.

A joint effort. Eysenck and his second wife, Sybil (Ph.D., University of London), developed many of their research questionnaires together. The Eysenck Personality Inventory (1963) took 12 years of joint research and 20 factor analyses. Hans acknowledged that, although published under both names, it was largely a monument to her skill, patience and endurance; the chapter notes how rare such open acknowledgement of a spouse's work is.

Three dimensions. Their theory is built on three dimensions, defined as combinations of traits or factors; they can be thought of as superfactors:
E: extraversion vs introversion.
N: neuroticism vs emotional stability.
P: psychoticism vs impulse control (or superego functioning).
Eysenck noted that extraversion and neuroticism have been recognised as basic elements of personality since the ancient Greek philosophers, and (1997) that versions of these dimensions appear on nearly every personality test ever devised. The Eysenck Personality Inventory has been used successfully in translation in nearly 40 countries, including Italy and Kuwait. Table 8.4 lists the traits of each: E (sociable, lively, active, assertive, sensation seeking, carefree, dominant, venturesome); N (anxious, depressed, guilt feelings, low self-esteem, tense, irrational, shy, moody); P (aggressive, cold, egocentric, impersonal, impulsive, antisocial, creative, tough-minded). High scorers on E are extraverts; low scorers are introverts.

Stability over time. Eysenck's traits and dimensions tend to stay stable across the life span despite changing social and environmental experiences: an introverted child tends to remain introverted into adulthood (Ganiban et al., 2008). Studies in England and Scandinavia confirm this stability, particularly for extraversion and neuroticism (Billstedt et al., 2014; Gale et al., 2013).

The role of intelligence. Eysenck researched intelligence extensively. He did not list it as a personality dimension but saw it as an important influence on personality: someone with an IQ of 120 is likely to have a more complex, multidimensional personality than someone with an IQ of 80. His research suggested that about 80 percent of intelligence is inherited and only 20 percent due to social and environmental forces (Eysenck & Eysenck, 1985).
sections.simple: Eysenck used factor analysis like Cattell but criticised it and added experiments. With his wife Sybil he built the Eysenck Personality Inventory and proposed three big 'superfactors': extraversion (E), neuroticism (N) and psychoticism (P). These stay fairly stable over life. He also thought intelligence, about 80 percent inherited, shapes how complex a personality is.
keyPoints: Agreed traits come from factor analysis but criticised its subjectivity; added tests and experiments.
Eysenck Personality Inventory (1963) with Sybil Eysenck: 12 years, 20 factor analyses.
Three superfactors: E (extraversion-introversion), N (neuroticism-emotional stability), P (psychoticism-impulse control).
Dimensions are stable over the life span, especially E and N.
Intelligence is not a dimension but influences personality; about 80% inherited.

sections.heading: Extraversion
sections.detailed:
Description. Extraverts are oriented toward the outside world, prefer the company of others, and tend to be sociable, impulsive, adventurous, assertive and dominant. Introverts are at the opposite pole of the E dimension.

Research correlates. People scoring high on extraversion on the Eysenck Personality Inventory experience more pleasant emotions and are happier than low scorers (Fisher & Francis, 2013; Holder & Klassen, 2010; Lucas & Fujita, 2000). Extraverted businessmen were much better at performing difficult tasks than introverted businessmen (Campbell et al., 2011).

Biological basis: cortical arousal. Eysenck was interested in how extraverts and introverts differ biologically and genetically. He found that extraverts have a lower base level of cortical arousal than introverts (Eysenck, 1990b). Because their arousal is low, extraverts need and actively seek excitement and stimulation. Introverts already have high cortical arousal, so they avoid excitement and stimulation.

Sensory sensitivity. As a result, introverts react more strongly than extraverts to sensory stimulation. Studies show introverts are more sensitive to low-level stimuli and have lower pain thresholds. Other research supports these differences in response to stimulation but finds less convincing evidence that they are due to differences in cortical arousal (Bullock & Gilliland, 1993; Hagemann & Naumann, 2009; Stelmack, 1997). Nevertheless, as Eysenck predicted, the differences are genetically based.

The arousal explanation is the classic 10-mark point: it explains behaviour (sociability vs withdrawal) by an inherited biological set-point, which fits the chapter's genetics approach. Note the qualification: the behavioural differences are well supported, but the arousal mechanism itself is less firmly established.
sections.simple: Extraverts are outgoing, sociable, impulsive and dominant, and research shows they are happier. Eysenck said extraverts have naturally low brain (cortical) arousal, so they seek excitement, while introverts are already highly aroused and avoid it. Introverts are more sensitive to stimulation and pain, and these differences are genetic, though the arousal explanation is less certain.
keyPoints: Extraverts are outward-oriented, sociable, impulsive, adventurous, assertive and dominant.
High E scorers report more pleasant emotions and happiness; extraverted businessmen did better on hard tasks.
Extraverts have lower base cortical arousal, so they seek stimulation; introverts avoid it.
Introverts are more sensitive to low-level stimuli and have lower pain thresholds.
Differences are genetic, though evidence linking them to arousal is less convincing.

sections.heading: Neuroticism
sections.detailed:
Description. Neurotics are anxious, depressed, tense, irrational and moody, and may have low self-esteem and be prone to guilt feelings (Table 8.4). Eysenck held that neuroticism is largely inherited, a product of genetics rather than learning or experience.

Research findings.
- A 2-year study of Americans aged 16 to 70 found that growing satisfaction from work and social relationships was linked to lower neuroticism and higher extraversion (Scollon & Diener, 2006).
- In Australia, high-neuroticism scorers on the Eysenck Personality Inventory outperformed low scorers when the work environment was fast-paced and stressful; neurotics seemed to function best in busy situations that forced them to work harder (Smillie et al., 2006).
- In England, people high in neuroticism scored lower in verbal abilities (Chamorro-Premuzic, Furnham, & Petrides, 2006).
- In Sweden, people high in neuroticism in middle age were much more likely to show cognitive impairment when retested 25 years later (Crowe et al., 2006).

Biological basis. People high in neuroticism have greater activity in brain areas that control the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, the body's alarm system that responds to stress or danger by raising breathing rate, heart rate, blood flow to the muscles and adrenaline release. Eysenck argued that in neurotics the sympathetic nervous system overreacts even to mild stressors, producing chronic hypersensitivity. This leads to heightened emotionality in almost any difficult situation; neurotics react emotionally to events others think trivial. According to Eysenck, these differences in biological reactivity are innate: people are genetically predisposed either toward neuroticism or toward emotional stability.
sections.simple: Neurotic people are anxious, moody, tense and low in self-esteem, and Eysenck thought this is mostly inherited. Their sympathetic nervous system (the body's alarm system) overreacts even to small stresses. Research shows neurotics can do well in fast, stressful jobs, but tend to have lower verbal ability and more cognitive decline later in life.
keyPoints: Neurotics: anxious, depressed, tense, irrational, moody, low self-esteem, guilt-prone.
Eysenck: neuroticism is largely inherited, not learned.
Scollon & Diener (2006): rising work/social satisfaction linked to lower N, higher E.
Smillie et al. (2006): neurotics outperformed in fast-paced stressful work; lower verbal ability (Chamorro-Premuzic et al.); later cognitive impairment (Crowe et al.).
Overactive sympathetic nervous system causes chronic hypersensitivity and heightened emotionality; this reactivity is innate.

sections.heading: Psychoticism
sections.detailed:
Description. High scorers on psychoticism are aggressive, antisocial, tough-minded, cold and egocentric. They have also been found to be cruel, hostile and insensitive to others' needs and feelings. They score low on emotional well-being and have more problems with alcohol, drug abuse and violent criminal behaviour than low scorers (Boduszek et al., 2013; Ciarrochi & Heaven, 2007; Sher, Bartholow, & Wood, 2000).

Creativity. Paradoxically, high scorers can also be very creative.

Genes and environment. The evidence suggests a large genetic component. However, high scorers had more authoritarian and controlling parents than low scorers, which supports a potentially harmful influence of the childhood environment (Heaven & Ciarrochi, 2006).

Sex differences and hormones. Men generally score higher than women, leading Eysenck to suggest that psychoticism may be related to male hormones.

Crime. Eysenck speculated that people high on all three dimensions may be prone to criminal behaviour, but he cited only modest empirical support (Eysenck & Gudjonsson, 1989). Research in China found a significant positive correlation between criminal behaviour and high scores on both psychoticism and neuroticism (Huo-Liang, 2006).

Society needs diversity. Eysenck believed society needs the variety provided by people at all points of the three dimensions. An ideal society lets people make the best use of their traits and abilities, though some will adapt better than others. A person high in psychoticism, typified by hostility and aggression, might become emotionally disturbed or criminal, or might channel aggressive traits into a socially acceptable enterprise such as coaching college football.

This section answers Review Question 13 (behaviour of high P scorers).
sections.simple: People high in psychoticism are aggressive, cold, egocentric and antisocial, and have more problems with alcohol, drugs and violent crime, yet they can also be very creative. The trait seems largely genetic, but controlling parents may make it worse. Men score higher, possibly due to male hormones, and Eysenck thought such people could also channel aggression into acceptable roles like coaching.
keyPoints: High P: aggressive, antisocial, tough-minded, cold, egocentric, cruel, hostile, insensitive.
Linked to low well-being and more alcohol, drug and violent crime problems.
Paradoxically creative; largely genetic, but authoritarian parents also linked (Heaven & Ciarrochi, 2006).
Men score higher, possibly due to male hormones; crime linked to high P and N (Huo-Liang, 2006).
Society needs diversity; high P can be channelled into acceptable roles such as coaching football.

sections.heading: The Primary Role of Heredity
sections.detailed:
Eysenck's position. Eysenck held that traits and dimensions are determined primarily by heredity, although the evidence shows a stronger genetic component for extraversion and neuroticism than for psychoticism. He did not rule out environmental and situational influences, such as family interactions in childhood, but believed their effects on personality were limited (Eysenck, 1990a).

Twin studies. His research compared identical (monozygotic) and fraternal (dizygotic) twins. Identical twins proved more alike in personality than fraternal twins, even when the identical twins had been reared by different parents in different environments during childhood. Since identical twins share all their genes and fraternal twins do not, greater similarity in identical twins (even when raised apart) points to heredity.

Adoption studies. Adopted children's personalities resemble those of their biological parents more than those of their adoptive parents, even when the children have had no contact with their biological parents. This gives further support to the idea that personality owes more to genetic inheritance than to environment.

Cross-cultural evidence. Eysenck's three dimensions have been found consistently in more than 35 nations, including the United States, England, Australia, Japan, China, Nigeria and Sweden (Bouchard, 1985; Eaves, Eysenck, & Martin, 1989; Floderus-Myrhed et al., 1980; Hur, 2009; Martin & Jardine, 1986; Tellegen et al., 1988). Finding the same three dimensions in very different cultures is taken as further evidence that inherited factors are primary in shaping personality.

This section directly answers Review Questions 11 and 14. The chapter's research highlights summarise Eysenck's support: extraverts experience more pleasant emotions and have lower cortical arousal; neurotics have low self-esteem and guilt, function well in fast-paced jobs and score lower in verbal ability; psychotics are cruel, hostile, insensitive, aggressive, antisocial and egocentric and have more alcohol and drug problems; and all three dimensions are determined primarily by heredity.
sections.simple: Eysenck believed personality is mainly inherited, especially extraversion and neuroticism. Identical twins are more alike than fraternal twins even when raised apart, and adopted children resemble their biological parents more than their adoptive ones. The same three dimensions appear in over 35 countries, which also suggests a genetic basis.
keyPoints: Traits and dimensions primarily inherited; genetic evidence stronger for E and N than P.
Environment (e.g. childhood family) has only limited effects.
Identical twins more alike than fraternal twins, even when reared apart.
Adopted children resemble biological more than adoptive parents.
Three dimensions found in 35+ nations, supporting the primacy of heredity.

sections.heading: Robert McCrae and Paul Costa: The Five-Factor Model; Measuring the Five Factors
sections.detailed:
Why five? Using factor analysis, Cattell and Eysenck arrived at different numbers of traits. The chapter says this is not a flaw in the method but reflects how each chose to measure personality. Some later researchers were dissatisfied with both, feeling Eysenck had too few dimensions (three) and Cattell too many factors (sixteen).

The Big Five. Working at the Gerontology Research Center of the National Institutes of Health in Baltimore, Robert McCrae (1949-) and Paul Costa (1942-) began an extensive research programme in the 1980s that identified five robust, or Big Five, factors (McCrae & Costa, 1985b, 1987): neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness. After more than 25 years and hundreds of studies, McCrae (2011) described the model as a turning point in the history of personality psychology.

The factors and their traits (Table 8.5):
Neuroticism: worried, insecure, nervous, highly strung.
Extraversion: sociable, talkative, fun-loving, affectionate.
Openness: original, independent, creative, daring.
Agreeableness: good-natured, softhearted, trusting, courteous.
Conscientiousness: careful, reliable, hardworking, organised.

Measuring the factors. The factors were confirmed by several assessment techniques: self-ratings, objective tests and observers' reports. McCrae and Costa then built the NEO Personality Inventory (NEO-PI), named from the initials of the first three factors (Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness); it exists in several revised forms. A shorter version was developed for research on the Internet (Buchanan, Johnson, & Goldberg, 2005). Because the same factors appear across different assessment methods, they can be relied on as distinguishing aspects of personality.

Other measures. Following McCrae and Costa, other researchers produced quicker adjective checklists on which subjects select the words that best describe themselves; one uses 100 adjectives and another only 40. Even so, the NEO remains the most frequently used measure. Like all self-report inventories, however, its results can be distorted by subjects who deliberately try to appear psychologically well adjusted.
sections.simple: Some researchers felt Eysenck's three dimensions were too few and Cattell's sixteen too many. McCrae and Costa found five robust factors: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness (the Big Five). They measured them with the NEO Personality Inventory, still the most used test, though like any self-report it can be faked.
keyPoints: Eysenck's 3 seemed too few and Cattell's 16 too many; the difference reflects measurement choices.
McCrae and Costa (NIH Gerontology Research Center, 1980s) identified the Big Five: N, E, O, A, C.
Factors confirmed by self-ratings, objective tests and observer reports.
NEO Personality Inventory named from Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness; short Internet version exists.
Adjective checklists (100 or 40 words) are quicker, but the NEO is most used; it can be faked.

sections.heading: Origin and Overlap of Factors
sections.detailed:
Origin: heredity vs environment. Twin studies found that four of the five factors have a stronger hereditary component: neuroticism, extraversion, openness and conscientiousness. Agreeableness was found to have a stronger environmental component (Bergeman et al., 1993; Pedersen, Plomin, McClearn, & Friberg, 1988). This directly answers the part of Review Question 15 about the role of heredity and environment in each factor. The chapter summary calls the five factors biologically based.

Overlap with other theories. The model overlaps with earlier concepts:
- McCrae and Costa's extraversion and neuroticism are similar to Eysenck's extraversion and neuroticism dimensions.
- Agreeableness and conscientiousness may represent the low end of Eysenck's psychoticism dimension, that is, the impulse-control pole. In other words, someone low in psychoticism would tend to be agreeable and conscientious.
- Openness correlates highly and positively with intelligence.
- Agreeableness correlates with Alfred Adler's concept of social interest (discussed in Chapter 4).

Why this matters. The overlaps show convergence among independent approaches: the same broad dimensions keep reappearing, which strengthens confidence that they are real features of personality rather than artefacts of one researcher's method. The heritability findings place the model firmly within the genetics approach, while the environmental basis of agreeableness reminds us that not every factor is equally inherited.
sections.simple: Twin studies show neuroticism, extraversion, openness and conscientiousness are mainly inherited, while agreeableness depends more on environment. The Big Five overlaps with older ideas: E and N match Eysenck's, agreeableness and conscientiousness look like low psychoticism, openness goes with intelligence, and agreeableness resembles Adler's social interest.
keyPoints: N, E, O and C have a stronger hereditary component (twin studies).
Agreeableness has a stronger environmental component.
E and N resemble Eysenck's E and N dimensions.
A and C may represent the low (impulse-control) end of Eysenck's psychoticism.
Openness correlates highly with intelligence; agreeableness with Adler's social interest.

sections.heading: Cross-Cultural Consistency and the Relative Value of the Factors in Different Cultures
sections.detailed:
Cross-cultural consistency. The five factors have been observed consistently in Eastern and Western cultures, which also supports a genetic component. McCrae and Costa (1997) described them as a common human structure of personality that transcends cultural differences. The factors and their traits have been found in more than 50 nations, including Britain, Germany, Portugal, the Czech Republic, Turkey, Israel, China, Korea, Japan, France, the Philippines, Russia, India, Denmark, Italy, Lebanon, Canada and Romania, and among both native-born and Hispanic residents of the United States (Allik et al., 2009; Heine & Buchtel, 2009; Ispas et al., 2014).

An important limitation. The countries where the factors have been measured tend to be urban, literate and well educated. An extensive study of a small, isolated, largely illiterate tribal group in a remote area of Bolivia found no evidence of the five factors (Gurven et al., 2013). This qualifies claims of universality.

Relative value of the factors. Although the same factors appear in virtually all urban cultures, cultures differ in how important and socially desirable each factor is:
- Australians see extraversion and agreeableness as more desirable than the other three.
- Japanese rate conscientiousness above all others, more important even than emotional stability.
- In Hong Kong and India, agreeableness is the most important factor.
- In Singapore, emotional stability matters most.
- In Venezuela, extraversion is the main characteristic to praise.
- In Chile, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Turkey and the United States, no single factor stood out.
Overall, Europeans and Americans tended to score higher in extraversion and openness and lower in agreeableness than Asians and Africans (Allik & McCrae, 2004; McCrae & Terracciano, 2005).

For exams, note the distinction between the structure of personality (largely the same across urban cultures) and the value placed on each factor (which varies by culture).
sections.simple: The Big Five has been found in more than 50 countries, East and West, suggesting a common human personality structure, though not in an isolated, illiterate tribe in Bolivia. Cultures value the factors differently: Japan prizes conscientiousness, India and Hong Kong agreeableness, Singapore emotional stability and Venezuela extraversion.
keyPoints: Big Five found in 50+ nations, East and West: a 'common human structure' (McCrae & Costa, 1997).
Cross-cultural consistency supports a genetic component.
Not found in an isolated, largely illiterate Bolivian tribe (Gurven et al., 2013).
Valued factor differs: Australia E and A; Japan C; Hong Kong and India A; Singapore emotional stability; Venezuela E.
Europeans and Americans higher in E and O, lower in A, than Asians and Africans.

sections.heading: Gender Differences; How People View Themselves and Others
sections.detailed:
Gender differences. Sex differences in the five factors appear consistent. Research in 55 countries, Eastern and Western, found that women reported higher levels of neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness than men. Interestingly, these differences were most pronounced in prosperous, egalitarian nations where women had more opportunities for education and employment (Schmitt, Realo, Voracek, & Allik, 2008). This is counterintuitive: one might expect sex differences to shrink where the sexes are more equal, but they were larger.

How people view themselves and others. There is cross-cultural consistency in how people perceive their own and others' personalities. People tend to see themselves as more neurotic and more open to experience than others see them. They also tend to see others as higher in conscientiousness than they believe themselves to be (Allik et al., 2010). The research highlights box summarises this as seeing others as more conscientious and less neurotic than ourselves.

These findings matter for assessment: self-ratings and observer ratings of the same person can differ systematically, which is one reason the five factors were confirmed with both self-ratings and observers' reports.
sections.simple: Across 55 countries, women reported higher neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness than men, especially in rich, equal societies. People also tend to see themselves as more neurotic and open than others see them, and see others as more conscientious than themselves.
keyPoints: 55 countries: women higher in N, E, A and C than men (Schmitt et al., 2008).
Sex differences largest in prosperous, egalitarian nations.
People see themselves as more neurotic and open than others see them.
People see others as more conscientious than themselves (Allik et al., 2010).

sections.heading: Stability of the Factors over Time; Predicting Changes over Time
sections.detailed:
The chapter warns that the many stability studies may seem contradictory, and that results vary by country and especially by the age range and time span studied.

Evidence of stability.
- The five factors are found in children as well as adults.
- A 6-year longitudinal study showed high stability for all five factors (Costa & McCrae, 1988); those high in agreeableness as children tended to remain so as adults.
- In Finland, twins aged 18 to 59 showed high stability for both sexes on extraversion and neuroticism across that 40-year span (Viken et al., 1994).
- American men and women followed from late adolescence into adulthood showed modest but significant stability for extraversion and neuroticism (Carmichael & McGue, 1994).
- College graduates tested for extraversion as students and 20 years later showed a significant positive correlation: extraverted students remained extraverted at midlife, and high scorers were more sociable and outgoing (Von Dras & Siegler, 1997).
- A large US study with measures 40 years apart found extraversion and conscientiousness the most stable (Hampson & Goldberg, 2006).

Evidence of change.
- American and Belgian adolescents over 4 years: extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness were stable, but openness increased for both sexes (McCrae et al., 2002).
- From adolescence to adulthood in the Czech Republic and Russia, neuroticism, extraversion and openness declined while agreeableness and conscientiousness rose (McCrae et al., 2004a, 2004b).
- German adults tested in their 40s and again in their 60s showed declining neuroticism (Allemand, Zimprich, & Hertzog, 2007).
- A large review found neuroticism, extraversion and openness decrease by the 60s, while agreeableness and conscientiousness increase with age (Debast et al., 2014).

Predicting changes over time. Preschool teachers predicted what their 3- to 6-year-olds would be like in 20 years; their expectations, based on observing the children, matched the students' Big Five scores, suggesting teachers assumed preschool behaviour would closely relate to adult behaviour (Graziano et al., 1998). The chapter raises a question: might such expectations lead teachers and parents to reinforce certain behaviours, strengthening genetically based characteristics? For example, do adults treat extraverted and introverted children differently in ways that strengthen their inherited tendencies? This hints at gene-environment interplay.

Overall: most factors are stable to some degree over the life span, but there is a general maturation trend toward lower N, E and O and higher A and C with age.
sections.simple: Many studies show the Big Five are fairly stable, especially extraversion and neuroticism; extraverted students are still extraverted 20 years later. But there are age trends: neuroticism, extraversion and openness tend to drop and agreeableness and conscientiousness rise as people get older. Preschool teachers could predict children's adult personalities, raising the question of whether adults reinforce inborn traits.
keyPoints: High stability of all five over 6 years (Costa & McCrae, 1988); E and N stable over 40 years in Finnish twins.
Extraverted students remained extraverted 20 years later (Von Dras & Siegler, 1997); E and C most stable over 40 years.
Openness rose in adolescents (McCrae et al., 2002); N, E, O fell and A, C rose from adolescence to adulthood.
N, E, O decrease and A, C increase by the 60s (Debast et al., 2014).
Preschool teachers' predictions matched Big Five scores (Graziano et al., 1998); adults may reinforce inherited tendencies.

sections.heading: Emotional Correlates: Well-Being, Happiness, Popularity and Success
sections.detailed:
Emotional well-being and happiness.
- Extraversion is positively, and neuroticism negatively, related to emotional well-being (Heller et al., 2004; Lischetzke & Eid, 2006). Researchers concluded that people high in extraversion and low in neuroticism are genetically predisposed to emotional stability (Costa & McCrae, 1984; Watson et al., 1992).
- College students high in extraversion coped better with everyday stress and were more likely to seek social support (Amirkhan, Risinger, & Swickert, 1995).
- The depression facet of neuroticism and the positive emotions/cheerfulness facet of extraversion are the most consistent predictors of life satisfaction and well-being (Schimmack et al., 2004).
- Teenagers in the US, Brazil and Italy: extraversion related to happiness, optimism and life satisfaction; openness, conscientiousness and low neuroticism also contributed to positive feelings (Bassi et al., 2014; Suldo et al., 2014; Zanon et al., 2014).
- High agreeableness and conscientiousness are linked to greater well-being (McCrae & Costa, 1991). High agreeableness is linked to being cooperative, helpful, altruistic, honest and selfless (Digman, 1990; John, 1990).
- Workers in China: extraversion, conscientiousness and low neuroticism related to subjective well-being (Zhai et al., 2013).
- High neuroticism is associated with psychological distress (DeRaad, 2000; Larsen & Kasimatis, 1991; Ormel & Wohlfarth, 1991) and with proneness to depression, anxiety, substance abuse and self-blame (Jorm, 1987; Kotov et al., 2010; Parkes, 1986).
- In Germany, high neuroticism and openness were linked to greater suicide risk; lowest risk was among those high in extraversion and conscientiousness (Bluml et al., 2013).

Popularity and success.
