- US college students high in extraversion enjoyed higher status and prominence among peers (Anderson et al., 2001). Extraverts rated social situations positive only if pleasant, showing the importance of positive emotion in extraversion (Lucas & Diener, 2001).
- Fifth to eighth graders high in conscientiousness were more accepted by peers, had more and better friendships and were less often targets of aggression (Jensen-Campbell & Malcolm, 2007).
- Over 4 years, extraverted college students experienced more positive events (good grades, pay rises, marriage), while high-neuroticism students experienced more negative events (illness, weight gain, traffic tickets, graduate school rejection) (Magnus et al., 1993).
- US adults aged 25 to 74: everyday stressors had much stronger negative emotional effects for high-neuroticism people (Mroczek & Almeida, 2004).
- Swedish twins reared together and apart: women high in extraversion and openness had more positive life events; women high in neuroticism had more negative ones (Saudino et al., 1997).
- Dutch teenagers high in extraversion, emotional stability and agreeableness were judged more popular and likeable by classmates (Van der Linden et al., 2010).
- In the US, people high in extraversion and agreeableness were rated more physically attractive (Meier et al., 2010).

These findings answer Review Question 17's emotional side for neuroticism: distress, depression, anxiety, substance abuse, self-blame, suicide risk, negative life events and stronger reactions to daily stress.
sections.simple: Extraverts tend to be happier, cope better with stress, are more popular and experience more good events, while people high in neuroticism suffer more distress, depression, anxiety and bad events. Agreeable and conscientious people also show more well-being, and conscientious children have better friendships.
keyPoints: Extraversion relates positively, and neuroticism negatively, to well-being; high E/low N predisposed to stability.
Extraverts cope better with stress, seek social support, and enjoy higher status and more positive events.
High N: distress, depression, anxiety, substance abuse, self-blame, negative events, higher suicide risk (with O).
Agreeableness and conscientiousness linked to well-being; conscientious children better accepted by peers.
High E, emotional stability and A judged more popular; high E and A rated more attractive.

sections.heading: Behavioral Correlates: Personal Characteristics and Physical Health
sections.detailed:
Personal characteristics.
- High openness: wide intellectual interests, seeking challenges, more likely to change jobs, try different careers and expect varied experiences (McCrae & Costa, 1985a, 1985b). High openness plus extraversion: more likely to be self-employed. Extraverts are also more active and satisfied in retirement (Lockenhoff et al., 2009; Robinson et al., 2010; Shane et al., 2010).
- High conscientiousness: reliable, responsible, punctual, efficient, dependable, and better school grades (Back et al., 2006; Chowdhury & Amin, 2006; Wagerman & Funder, 2007). British students high in conscientiousness were more organised, self-disciplined and achievement oriented in planning future goals (Conner & Abraham, 2001).
- Agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness correlate positively with college grades (Poropat, 2009); high scorers on these three were also rated better parents and better at coping with stress (Carver & Connor-Smith, 2010; Prinzie et al., 2009).
- At work, high conscientiousness predicts setting high goals and striving for them, initiating desirable behaviour and receiving high performance ratings; it is a valid predictor of job performance in professional, police, managerial, sales and skilled labour jobs (Barrick & Mount, 1996; Barrick, Mount, & Strauss, 1993; Stewart et al., 1996).

Physical health.
- Conscientious people tend to be healthier and live longer (Friedman & Martin, 2011).
- Conscientious adult smokers were less likely to smoke at home, suggesting awareness of indoor health risks to themselves and others (Hampson et al., 2000).
- Conscientious US college students wear seat belts, exercise, sleep enough and eat more fruit and vegetables (Raynor & Levine, 2009).
- Young people with diabetes who were more conscientious sought more information and were more diligent about self-care (Skinner et al., 2002).
- Conscientious British students showed far fewer hypochondriacal complaints (Ferguson, 2000); conscientious US adults took more responsibility for healthy behaviour (Tucker, Elliott, & Klein, 2006).
- People with ADHD who were higher in agreeableness had significantly lower hyperactivity, impulsivity, inattention and disorganisation (Nigg et al., 2002).
- Patients with chronic renal insufficiency who scored higher in neuroticism on the NEO had a 37.5 percent higher mortality rate over 4 years (Christensen et al., 2002).
- Contradictory neuroticism findings: high neuroticism predicted poorer physical health and well-being in old age but also greater longevity, so neurotics may live longer but are not happy about it (Eysenck, 2009; Friedman, Kern, & Reynolds, 2010). High neuroticism was also linked to fewer dementia-type cognitive declines in old age (Williams, Suchy, & Kraybill, 2010).
- Two large US studies: higher extraversion linked to greater stroke risk; high conscientiousness to lower risk of death from stroke and coronary heart disease; high neuroticism to more heart disease (Jokela et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
- In Australia and Finland, high extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness meant more and better sleep, while high neuroticism meant worse sleep (Hintsanen et al., 2014).
- In Korea, overweight to obese men were high in openness and low in conscientiousness; overweight women were low in neuroticism and openness (Shim et al., 2014).

Conscientiousness emerges as the strongest positive predictor of achievement and health, answering Review Question 16's conscientiousness part.
sections.simple: Open people seek variety and change jobs more; conscientious people are reliable, get better grades, perform better at work and live healthier, longer lives. Neuroticism has mixed health effects: worse health and a higher death rate in kidney patients, but also longer life and less dementia in some studies. Extraversion was linked to more stroke risk.
keyPoints: Openness: broad interests, career change; openness plus extraversion linked to self-employment.
Conscientiousness: reliability, better grades, high goals, job performance across many occupations.
A, C and O together predict better grades, parenting and coping (Poropat, 2009).
Conscientious people are healthier and live longer; seat belts, exercise, sleep, diet, diabetes self-care.
Neuroticism: 37.5% higher mortality in renal patients, heart disease, poor sleep, yet greater longevity and less dementia; extraversion linked to stroke risk.

sections.heading: Behavioral Correlates: Addictive and Criminal Behavior, Social Relationships, and Comment
sections.detailed:
Addictive and criminal behaviour.
- Adults low in conscientiousness and agreeableness were far more likely to be heavy users of alcohol or illegal drugs (Walton & Roberts, 2004).
- Among sexual minorities, those high in extraversion and conscientiousness were likely to show high drug and alcohol use (Livingston et al., 2014).
- Young adults high in neuroticism and openness were more likely to use prescription drugs not prescribed for them (Benotsch et al., 2013).
- A 25-year Finnish study: high agreeableness meant less alcoholism, less depression, fewer arrests and more career stability (Laursen, Pulkkinen, & Adams, 2002).
- Irish adolescents: agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism and extraversion were linked to criminal behaviour (O'Riordan & O'Connell, 2014).
- Norwegian students: neuroticism linked to Internet addiction, exercise addiction, compulsive buying and study addiction; extraversion linked to Facebook and smartphone addiction, exercise addiction and compulsive buying (Andreassen et al., 2013).

Social relationships.
- An 18-month study of German first-year university students: extraverts made more friends and were more likely to fall in love; agreeable students had less conflict with opposite-sex acquaintances; conscientious students kept more contact with parents and siblings; openness had no significant effect (Asendorpf & Wilpers, 1998).
- German high school graduates who stayed with parents were low in openness; those living with roommates increased in openness; those living with a romantic partner increased in conscientiousness (Jonkmann et al., 2013).
- Dutch couples: low neuroticism and high extraversion in both partners related to marital happiness (Barelds, 2005).
- US newlyweds: over two years self-rated agreeableness and conscientiousness rose and neuroticism fell, but spouses' ratings showed declines in conscientiousness, agreeableness, extraversion and openness; people thought they were improving, their partners disagreed (Watson & Humrichouse, 2006).
- College students who wanted higher economic, social and political status scored high in extraversion and low in agreeableness (Roberts & Robins, 2000).
- Dog people score higher in extraversion, agreeableness and conscientiousness and lower in neuroticism and openness than cat people (Gosling, Sandy, & Potter, 2010).

Comment. Studies of a wide range of emotions and behaviours show the five-factor model has high predictive value. Most research uses the five broad factors rather than their component traits. Comparisons found that both higher-level factors and lower-level traits predict well, but the narrower traits had higher validities (Paunonen, 1998; Paunonen & Ashton, 2001). McCrae and Costa's findings have been replicated and continue to inspire research, giving a well-supported view of personality and of heredity vs environment, though not all psychologists agree these are the only factors in personality, which leads to HEXACO.

Research highlights (p. 238): high extraversion goes with emotional stability, life satisfaction, coping, good grades and status; high conscientiousness with reliability, better grades, organisation, high goals, peer acceptance, health, longevity and healthy habits; high C, A, O and E together with popularity, attractiveness, grades, coping, good parenting and preferring dogs.
sections.simple: Low conscientiousness and agreeableness go with heavy drinking and drug use, while high agreeableness protects against alcoholism and arrests. Extraverts make more friends and fall in love more, and couples low in neuroticism are happier. Overall the Big Five predicts behaviour well, though narrow traits predict even better than the broad factors.
keyPoints: Low C and A predict heavy alcohol/drug use; high A predicts less alcoholism and fewer arrests over 25 years.
Neuroticism linked to Internet, exercise, study addiction and compulsive buying; extraversion to Facebook/smartphone addiction.
Extraverts make more friends and fall in love; agreeable people have less conflict; conscientious ones keep family contact; openness had no effect.
Low N and high E in both partners predict marital happiness; newlyweds see themselves improving, spouses disagree.
Model has high predictive value; narrow traits predict better than broad factors (Paunonen).

sections.heading: Michael Ashton and Kibeom Lee: HEXACO: The Six-Factor Model
sections.detailed:
The model. Michael Ashton (Brock University, Ontario) and Kibeom Lee (University of Calgary, Alberta) proposed a six-factor model of personality (2007, 2009). Two of its factors, extraversion and conscientiousness, are similar to those of the five-factor model; the other four differ to various degrees and are unique to this model (Ashton & Lee, 2008; Shepherd & Belicki, 2008). HEXACO is an acronym from the factors' initials. The chapter summary highlights that HEXACO adds honesty/humility to the five-factor model.

The six factors (Table 8.6):
Honesty/humility: sincere, honest, faithful vs greedy, pretentious, hypocritical, boastful.
Emotionality: emotional, oversensitive, anxious vs brave, tough, self-assured, stable.
eXtraversion: outgoing, lively, sociable, cheerful vs shy, passive, withdrawn, reserved.
Agreeableness: tolerant, peaceful, gentle vs quarrelsome, stubborn, ill-tempered.
Conscientiousness: disciplined, diligent, thorough, precise vs reckless, lazy, irresponsible, absent-minded.
Openness to experience: creative, innovative, unconventional vs shallow, conventional, unimaginative.

How it differs from the Big Five (Review Question 18). It has six rather than five factors; the new honesty/humility factor is the key addition; emotionality replaces neuroticism as a related but different factor; and agreeableness and openness differ in degree from their Big Five counterparts, while extraversion and conscientiousness are similar.

Assessing the six factors. Two self-report inventories exist: the 100-item HEXACO Personality Inventory, Revised (HEXACO-PI-R) and the 60-item HEXACO-60, both shown to be valid and reliable (Ashton & Lee, 2009). The factors have been documented in Dutch, French, German, Hungarian, Italian, Korean, Polish, Greek, Croatian, Turkish and Filipino cultures (Ashton et al., 2004, 2006; DeRaad & Barelds, 2008), more than a dozen cultures in the chapter summary's words.

Research on correlates (ongoing).
- In Italy, high conscientiousness was linked to voting for right-wing parties; left-wing voters scored higher in honesty, agreeableness and openness (Chirumbolo & Leone, 2010).
- New Zealand students low in openness and emotionality scored high in right-wing authoritarianism and prejudice toward dissident groups (Sibley et al., 2010).
- Employed Americans high in honesty/humility received higher job performance ratings (Johnson, Rowatt, & Petrini, 2011).
- Research in Egypt (Aghababaei) found honesty/humility correlated with stronger religious feelings but not with happiness; among Portuguese college students it did correlate with happiness (Oliveira, 2013).
- Adult delinquents in England and convicted criminals in Australia scored low on honesty/humility and high on Eysenck's psychoticism (Dunlop et al., 2012; Rollison, Hanoch, & Gummerum, 2013).
sections.simple: Ashton and Lee's HEXACO model has six factors: honesty/humility, emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness. Its big addition is honesty/humility. It is measured by the HEXACO-PI-R (100 items) or HEXACO-60, works in many cultures, and honesty/humility predicts better job ratings and less crime.
keyPoints: Six factors: Honesty/humility, Emotionality, eXtraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness.
Extraversion and conscientiousness resemble the Big Five; the other four differ; honesty/humility is the main addition.
Measured by the 100-item HEXACO-PI-R and the 60-item HEXACO-60, both valid and reliable.
Documented in Dutch, French, German, Hungarian, Italian, Korean, Polish, Greek, Croatian, Turkish and Filipino cultures.
Honesty/humility: higher job ratings, religious feelings; low in delinquents and criminals (with high psychoticism).

sections.heading: Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams: The Dark Triad of Personality
sections.detailed:
The model. Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams of the University of British Columbia introduced (2002) a three-factor approach to the darker side of personality:
- Narcissism: extreme selfishness, an inflated sense of one's abilities and talents, and a constant need for admiration and attention.
- Machiavellianism: the need to manipulate others, marked by cunning, deceit and unscrupulous behaviour.
- Psychopathy: callous, insensitive, egocentric and antisocial, taking advantage of others with great charm and often violence.

Assessing the Dark Triad. The Dirty Dozen Scale (Jonason & Webster, 2010) is a quick 12-item self-rating test. Its items cover manipulating others, using deceit or lies, using flattery and exploiting others to get one's way (Machiavellian items); lacking remorse, being unconcerned with the morality of one's actions, being callous or insensitive and being cynical (psychopathy items); and wanting admiration, wanting attention, seeking prestige or status and expecting special favours (narcissism items).

Behavioural correlates.
- High scorers on all three traits engage in more antisocial activities and take more satisfaction in others' misfortune (James et al., 2014; Porter et al., 2014).
- They show strong self-promotion and tend to be cold, duplicitous and aggressive (Paulhus & Webster, 2010).
- The verbal content of Facebook updates validly predicted levels of psychopathy and narcissism; updates were emotionally cold, aggressive and highly self-promoting (Garcia & Silkstrom, 2014).
- High Machiavellianism and psychopathy scorers were low on the Big Five factors of conscientiousness, agreeableness and openness, and showed little empathy, high aggression, vengeful and unforgiving attitudes, and low emotional stability (Giammarco & Vernon, 2014; Muris et al., 2013; Oliveira, 2013).
- The Dark Triad is associated with short-term exploitative sexual relationships. Psychopathy is linked to a high sex drive with strong sexual and sadomasochistic themes and fantasies; high psychopathy and narcissism scorers engaged in many short-term sexual relationships with no intention of commitment (Adams et al., 2014; Baughman et al., 2014).

The summary concludes that the Dark Triad can lead to antisocial, duplicitous and aggressive behaviour (answering Review Question 19). Note the link the chapter reports: Machiavellianism and psychopathy go with low Big Five agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness; the descriptions of psychopathy (callous, egocentric, antisocial) also echo the traits Eysenck lists for psychoticism.
sections.simple: Paulhus and Williams described three dark traits: narcissism (self-centred need for admiration), Machiavellianism (manipulation and deceit) and psychopathy (callous, charming, antisocial). They can be measured quickly with the 12-item Dirty Dozen. People high in these traits are more antisocial, aggressive and self-promoting, enjoy others' misfortune and prefer short-term sexual relationships.
keyPoints: Dark Triad (Paulhus & Williams, 2002): narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy.
Narcissism: selfishness, inflated self-view, need for admiration; Machiavellianism: manipulation, deceit; psychopathy: callous, charming, often violent.
Dirty Dozen Scale (Jonason & Webster, 2010): quick 12-item self-rating.
High scorers: antisocial, enjoy others' misfortune, self-promoting, cold, duplicitous, aggressive; Facebook posts reveal it.
Low C, A, O and empathy; linked to short-term exploitative sexual relationships.

sections.heading: Personality Traits and the Internet
sections.detailed:
Building on Chapter 1's point that the Internet, especially social networking, can both influence and reflect personality, the chapter reviews how the traits discussed affect Internet use.

Eysenck's dimensions.
- German college students: Internet addiction was greater among those high in neuroticism and excessively self-focused (Montag, Jurkiewicz, & Reuter, 2010).
- Turkish college students high in psychoticism used the Internet as a substitute for face-to-face interaction; often their friendships existed only online (Tosun & Lajunen, 2010).

Five-factor model.
- Israel: high conscientiousness meant more Facebook friends; highly neurotic people posted more of their photos (Amichai-Hamburger & Vinitzky, 2010).
- Finland: high extraversion meant more Facebook friends (Lonnqvist et al., 2014).
- Netherlands: near-compulsive, addictive Internet use was greatest among introverted, disagreeable, emotionally less stable and lonely adolescents (Van der Aa et al., 2009).
- Germany: video gaming addiction was highest among those high in neuroticism and low in conscientiousness and extraversion (Muller et al., 2014).
- US and Germany: students high in conscientiousness, agreeableness and emotional stability were far less likely to post about personal matters like substance abuse or sex; overall, American students were more inclined to post such content than Germans regardless of personality (Karl, Peluchette, & Schlaegel, 2010).
- American adults high in extraversion used social media more (Mark & Ganzach, 2014); American men high in emotional instability were even more likely to use these sites (Correa, Hinsley, & deZuniga, 2010).
- Taiwan: conscientious students shopped online for convenience, open students for adventure, neurotic students to avoid other people (Huang & Yang, 2010).
- Australia: adults high in extraversion, low in conscientiousness and socially lonely were more likely to use Facebook (Ryan & Xenos, 2011).
- Americans aged 11 to 16 high in openness spent more time on computers and video games (Witt, Massman, & Jackson, 2011).
- American college students who sent suggestive photos (sexting) were high in neuroticism and low in agreeableness (Delevi & Weisskirch, 2013).

Takeaway (Review Question 20). Traits shape how we interact on social networking sites, our risk of Internet and gaming addiction, what we post, and our online shopping motives. Neuroticism and low conscientiousness recur as risk factors for problematic use; extraversion predicts more online sociability.
sections.simple: Personality shapes how we use the Internet. Neurotic people are more prone to Internet and gaming addiction, post more photos and shop online to avoid people. Extraverts and conscientious people have more Facebook friends, open people shop online for adventure and play more games, and low agreeableness plus high neuroticism predicts sexting.
keyPoints: Eysenck: high neuroticism linked to Internet addiction; high psychoticism to online-only friendships.
More Facebook friends with high conscientiousness (Israel) and high extraversion (Finland).
Addictive Internet/gaming use linked to neuroticism, introversion, disagreeableness, low conscientiousness, loneliness.
Online shopping motives: C for convenience, O for adventure, N to avoid people (Taiwan).
Sexting linked to high N and low A; high C, A and emotional stability post less personal content.

sections.heading: Reflections on the Trait Approach
sections.detailed:
Heredity's share. The theories and research in the chapter suggest that inheritance may account for as much as 50 percent of personality (Brody, 1997; Buss, 1988; Stelmack, 1997). The evidence is strongest for extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, but almost every other dimension studied shows a strong biological component. (Compare Cattell's earlier estimate of one-third.)

Shared family environment. In many cases the shared family environment has only a minor influence. Some researchers take a harder line, arguing that twins, whether reared together or apart, will be alike in all facets of personality regardless of the family they grew up in, implying that genetic effects far outweigh environmental ones.

Implications. This has practical and theoretical consequences for personality psychology, which traditionally concentrated on family and social interaction in early childhood. Findings from behavioral genetics may require research to be restructured if personality development is to be fully explained.

A caution. We must not prematurely conclude that family and other environmental factors can be dismissed. The components of personality remain products of both genetic makeup and life experience, and psychologists' task is to determine the relative importance of each.

Overall evaluation of the chapter's approach. Strengths: rigorous measurement through factor analysis; replicated findings across cultures; strong predictive value for emotions, health, achievement, relationships and online behaviour; widely used instruments (16 PF, EPI, NEO-PI, HEXACO inventories, Dirty Dozen). Limitations: disagreement over the number of factors (3, 5, 6, 16), subjectivity in factor analysis, vulnerability of self-reports to faking, cultural limits (e.g. the Bolivian tribe), and the risk of underestimating environment.
sections.simple: The research suggests heredity may explain up to half of personality, especially extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, and that shared family environment often matters little. This challenges theories focused on early family life. But environment cannot be ignored: personality comes from both genes and experience, and the job is to work out how much each contributes.
keyPoints: Inheritance may account for up to 50% of personality (Brody, 1997; Buss, 1988; Stelmack, 1997).
Evidence strongest for E, N and P, but nearly all dimensions show a strong biological component.
Shared family environment often has only a minor influence; some argue twins are alike regardless of upbringing.
Behavioral genetics may require restructuring research that focused on early family interaction.
Environment cannot be discounted; personality reflects both genes and experience.

terms.definition: A statistical technique that correlates every pair of measures taken from a group to find a smaller number of underlying factors; highly correlated measures are combined into one factor.
Relatively permanent reaction tendencies, derived by factor analysis, that are the basic structural units or mental elements of personality.
Traits that everyone possesses to some degree, such as intelligence, extraversion and gregariousness, because people share similar heredity and social pressures.
Traits possessed by one or a few people, especially visible in interests and attitudes (e.g. a passion for genealogy).
Traits describing our skills and how efficiently we can work toward our goals; intelligence is an example.
Traits describing the general style and emotional tone of our behaviour, such as being assertive, easygoing or irritable.
Traits describing our motivations, interests and ambitions; the driving forces of behaviour.

Characteristics that correlate with one another but do not form a factor because they have no single source; less stable and less important (e.g. neuroticism made of anxiety, indecision and irrational fear).
Stable, permanent, unitary factors of personality derived by factor analysis, which combine to account for surface traits.
Source traits that originate in biological or physiological conditions, though not necessarily innate (e.g. behaviour resulting from alcohol use).
Source traits learned from social and physical environmental influences, imposing a pattern on personality.
Cattell's objective test measuring the 16 source traits in people aged 16 and older; used for research, clinical diagnosis and predicting job success.
Life-record data: observers' ratings of specific overt behaviours in real-life settings such as a classroom or office.
Self-report questionnaire ratings of one's own characteristics, attitudes and interests; vulnerable to poor self-awareness and faking.
Data from 'objective' personality tests that resist faking because the person does not know what is being measured.
The standard laboratory experiment in which one independent variable is manipulated to observe its effect on a dependent variable; Cattell found it too restrictive.
Case studies, dream analysis, free association and similar techniques; Cattell considered it subjective and unquantifiable.
Cattell's preferred research method, using factor analysis of many variables to yield highly specific data.
A form of factor analysis that collects large amounts of data from a group of people and correlates all scores to find traits.
A form of factor analysis that collects a large amount of data from a single subject over a long period.
The study of the relationship between genetic or hereditary factors and personality traits.
Eysenck's term for his personality dimensions, defined as combinations of traits or factors.
Eysenck's dimension: extraverts are sociable, lively, active, assertive, sensation seeking, carefree, dominant and venturesome; introverts are the low pole.
Eysenck's dimension: neurotics are anxious, depressed, guilt-prone, low in self-esteem, tense, irrational, shy and moody.
Eysenck's dimension (also called superego functioning): high scorers are aggressive, cold, egocentric, impersonal, impulsive, antisocial, creative and tough-minded.
Questionnaire developed by Hans and Sybil Eysenck (1963) over 12 years and 20 factor analyses; used in nearly 40 countries.
Base level of brain arousal; Eysenck found extraverts have lower levels and so seek stimulation, while introverts' high levels lead them to avoid it.
Branch of the autonomic nervous system acting as the body's alarm system; Eysenck argued it overreacts in neurotics, causing chronic hypersensitivity.
Identical (monozygotic) and fraternal (dizygotic) twins, compared by Eysenck to estimate the heritability of personality.
McCrae and Costa's model of five robust factors: neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness and conscientiousness.
McCrae and Costa's test of the five factors, named from the initials of neuroticism, extraversion and openness; the most frequently used Big Five measure.
Factor describing people who are worried, insecure, nervous and highly strung.
Factor describing people who are sociable, talkative, fun-loving and affectionate.
Factor describing people who are original, independent, creative and daring; correlates highly with intelligence.
Factor describing people who are good-natured, softhearted, trusting and courteous; has a stronger environmental component and correlates with Adler's social interest.
Factor describing people who are careful, reliable, hardworking and organised.
Quicker Big Five measures on which subjects pick words that describe themselves; one uses 100 adjectives, another 40.
Ashton and Lee's six-factor model: honesty/humility, emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness to experience.
HEXACO factor contrasting sincere, honest, faithful people with greedy, pretentious, hypocritical, boastful ones; the main addition to the five-factor model.
HEXACO factor contrasting emotional, oversensitive, anxious people with brave, tough, self-assured, stable ones.
The 100-item HEXACO Personality Inventory, Revised, and the 60-item HEXACO-60, both valid and reliable self-report measures of the six factors.
Paulhus and Williams' three-factor approach to the darker side of personality: narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy.
Extreme selfishness, an inflated sense of one's abilities and talents, and a constant need for admiration and attention.
The need to manipulate others, characterised by cunning, deceit and unscrupulous behaviour.
Being callous, insensitive, egocentric and antisocial, exploiting others with great charm and often violence.
A quick 12-item self-rating test of the Dark Triad developed by Jonason and Webster (2010).

people.name: Raymond Cattell
people.contribution: Applied factor analysis to normal people's personality to predict behaviour; classified traits, identified 16 source traits, built the 16 PF, proposed six life-span stages; regarded as father of the trait approach.

people.name: Charles E. Spearman
people.contribution: Psychologist-statistician who developed factor analysis and used it to measure mental abilities; supervised Cattell's graduate work at the University of London.

people.name: Edward L. Thorndike
people.contribution: Prominent American psychologist who invited Cattell to spend a year at his Columbia University laboratory, launching Cattell's American career.

people.name: Gordon Allport
people.contribution: Cattell's colleague at Harvard; with Cattell, among the first to propose that inherited factors shape personality and rank with environmental factors.

people.name: William Sheldon
people.contribution: Cattell's Harvard colleague who was developing a theory linking personality and body type.

people.name: J. Horn
people.contribution: Wrote (2001) that Cattell's theory was unrivalled in comprehensiveness and adherence to empirical evidence.

people.name: Sigmund Freud
people.contribution: Cattell, though not a Freudian, borrowed his ideas that the early years are crucial and that oral and anal conflicts affect personality.

people.name: Carl Jung
people.contribution: Cattell's late maturity stage (50-65), with its re-examination of values and search for a new self, is compared to Jung's view of midlife.

people.name: Hans Eysenck
people.contribution: Proposed three largely inherited superfactors (E, N, P), linked them to cortical arousal and nervous-system reactivity, and supported heritability with twin, adoption and cross-cultural research; world's most cited psychologist at his death.

people.name: Sybil Eysenck
people.contribution: Hans Eysenck's second wife (Ph.D., University of London); co-developed many questionnaires, and Hans credited the Eysenck Personality Inventory largely to her skill, patience and endurance.

people.name: Robert McCrae
people.contribution: With Paul Costa at the NIH Gerontology Research Center, identified the Big Five factors and developed the NEO Personality Inventory; called the model a turning point in personality psychology.

people.name: Paul Costa
people.contribution: Co-developer with McCrae of the five-factor model and NEO Personality Inventory; their research showed the factors' heritability, cross-cultural consistency and stability.

people.name: Alfred Adler
people.contribution: His concept of social interest correlates with the Big Five factor of agreeableness.

people.name: Michael Ashton
people.contribution: Brock University psychologist who, with Kibeom Lee, proposed the HEXACO six-factor model adding honesty/humility.

people.name: Kibeom Lee
people.contribution: University of Calgary psychologist, co-creator of the HEXACO model and its inventories (HEXACO-PI-R, HEXACO-60).

people.name: Delroy Paulhus
people.contribution: With Kevin Williams at the University of British Columbia, introduced the Dark Triad (2002) of narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy.

people.name: Kevin Williams
people.contribution: Co-introducer with Paulhus of the Dark Triad of personality.

people.name: Jonason and Webster
people.contribution: Developed the Dirty Dozen Scale (2010), a quick 12-item self-rating measure of the Dark Triad.

people.name: Paunonen
people.contribution: Showed (with Ashton) that both Big Five factors and lower-level traits predict behaviour, but narrower traits have higher validities.

studies.title: Cattell: twin and sibling comparisons
studies.finding: Comparing twins and non-twin siblings reared together and apart, about 80% of intelligence (B) and of timidity vs boldness (H) was genetic; overall one-third of personality is genetic and two-thirds environmental.

studies.title: Cattell (1982): 16 PF data on 3,000 males aged 12-18
studies.finding: Factors F, I and Q3 were determined mainly by heredity; Factors E, G and Q4 mainly by environment.

studies.title: Cattell & Nesselroade (1967): marital stability
studies.finding: 16 PF scores predicted marital stability: partners in stable marriages had similar traits, those in unstable marriages very different traits.

studies.title: Simon (2007): faking the 16 PF
studies.finding: College students, prisoners and substance abusers answering honestly and then favourably produced significantly different responses, showing the test can be faked.

studies.title: Van Eeden & Mantsha (2007): Tshivenda translation
studies.finding: Translation into Tshivenda in South Africa changed item meanings so much that responses were invalid; literal translation was impossible.

studies.title: Roussi-Vergou et al. (2009, 2011): Greek 16 PF
studies.finding: A satisfactory Greek translation clearly distinguished Greek elementary and preschool teachers from national population norms.

studies.title: Aksu et al. (2010): Turkish 16 PF
studies.finding: A Turkish translation was a valid measure of personality differences.

studies.title: Ganiban et al. (2008): stability of introversion
studies.finding: Introverted children tend to remain introverted through adolescence into adulthood.

studies.title: Billstedt et al. (2014); Gale et al. (2013): England and Scandinavia
studies.finding: Confirmed stability over time of Eysenck's dimensions, particularly extraversion and neuroticism.

studies.title: Eysenck & Eysenck (1985): heritability of intelligence
studies.finding: About 80% of intelligence is inherited and 20% due to social and environmental forces.

studies.title: Fisher & Francis (2013); Holder & Klassen (2010); Lucas & Fujita (2000)
studies.finding: High extraversion scorers on the Eysenck Personality Inventory experienced more pleasant emotions and were happier.

studies.title: Campbell et al. (2011): extraverted businessmen
studies.finding: Extraverted businessmen performed difficult tasks much better than introverted businessmen.

studies.title: Eysenck (1990b): cortical arousal
studies.finding: Extraverts have lower base cortical arousal, so seek stimulation; introverts' high arousal leads them to avoid it.

studies.title: Bullock & Gilliland (1993); Hagemann & Naumann (2009); Stelmack (1997)
studies.finding: Introverts are more sensitive to low-level stimuli and have lower pain thresholds, but evidence that this stems from cortical arousal is less convincing.

studies.title: Scollon & Diener (2006): Americans aged 16-70
studies.finding: Over 2 years, increasing satisfaction from work and relationships was associated with lower neuroticism and higher extraversion.

studies.title: Smillie et al. (2006): Australia
studies.finding: High-neuroticism people outperformed low scorers in fast-paced, stressful work environments.

studies.title: Chamorro-Premuzic, Furnham, & Petrides (2006): England
studies.finding: People high in neuroticism scored lower in verbal abilities.

studies.title: Crowe et al. (2006): Sweden
studies.finding: High neuroticism in middle age predicted much greater likelihood of cognitive impairment 25 years later.

studies.title: Boduszek et al. (2013); Ciarrochi & Heaven (2007); Sher et al. (2000)
studies.finding: High psychoticism scorers had low well-being and more problems with alcohol, drugs and violent crime.

studies.title: Heaven & Ciarrochi (2006): parenting and psychoticism
studies.finding: High psychoticism scorers had more authoritarian and controlling parents, suggesting harmful childhood environmental influence.

studies.title: Eysenck & Gudjonsson (1989): crime
studies.finding: Only modest support for the idea that people high on all three dimensions are prone to criminal behaviour.

studies.title: Huo-Liang (2006): China
studies.finding: Significant positive correlation between criminal behaviour and high psychoticism and neuroticism.

studies.title: Eysenck: twin and adoption studies
studies.finding: Identical twins were more alike than fraternal twins even when reared apart; adopted children resembled biological more than adoptive parents.

studies.title: Cross-cultural studies of Eysenck's dimensions (Bouchard, 1985; Tellegen et al., 1988 and others)
studies.finding: The three dimensions were found consistently in more than 35 nations, supporting the primacy of heredity.

studies.title: McCrae & Costa (1985b, 1987): the Big Five
studies.finding: Identified five robust factors (N, E, O, A, C), confirmed by self-ratings, objective tests and observer reports.

studies.title: Buchanan, Johnson, & Goldberg (2005)
studies.finding: Developed a shorter version of the five-factor inventory for Internet research.

studies.title: NEO faking research
studies.finding: NEO results, like all self-reports, can be distorted by subjects wanting to appear well adjusted.

studies.title: Bergeman et al. (1993); Pedersen et al. (1988): twin studies
studies.finding: N, E, O and C showed a stronger hereditary component; agreeableness a stronger environmental component.

studies.title: Allik et al. (2009); Heine & Buchtel (2009); Ispas et al. (2014)
studies.finding: The five factors were found in more than 50 nations and among native-born and Hispanic US residents.

studies.title: Gurven et al. (2013): Bolivian tribe
studies.finding: No evidence of the five factors in a small, isolated, largely illiterate tribal group in Bolivia.

studies.title: Allik & McCrae (2004); McCrae & Terracciano (2005): cultural value of factors
studies.finding: Cultures differ in which factor they value most; Europeans and Americans score higher in E and O and lower in A than Asians and Africans.

studies.title: Schmitt et al. (2008): 55 countries
studies.finding: Women reported higher N, E, A and C than men; differences largest in prosperous, egalitarian nations.

studies.title: Allik et al. (2010): self vs others
studies.finding: People see themselves as more neurotic and open than others see them, and see others as more conscientious than themselves.

studies.title: Costa & McCrae (1988): 6-year longitudinal study
studies.finding: High stability for all five factors; agreeable children tended to remain agreeable as adults.

studies.title: Viken et al. (1994): Finnish twins aged 18-59
studies.finding: High stability on extraversion and neuroticism for both sexes across a 40-year age span.

studies.title: Carmichael & McGue (1994)
studies.finding: Modest but significant stability of extraversion and neuroticism from late adolescence into adulthood.

studies.title: McCrae et al. (2002): American and Belgian adolescents
studies.finding: Over 4 years, E, A and C were stable but openness increased.

studies.title: Von Dras & Siegler (1997): college graduates
studies.finding: Extraversion scores in college correlated positively with scores 20 years later; extraverts remained sociable and outgoing.

studies.title: Hampson & Goldberg (2006): 40-year US study
studies.finding: Extraversion and conscientiousness were the most stable factors.

studies.title: McCrae et al. (2004a, 2004b): Czech Republic and Russia
studies.finding: From adolescence to adulthood, N, E and O declined while A and C rose.

studies.title: Allemand, Zimprich, & Hertzog (2007): Germany
studies.finding: Neuroticism declined between adults' 40s and 60s.

studies.title: Debast et al. (2014): research review
studies.finding: N, E and O decrease by the 60s, whereas A and C increase with age.

studies.title: Graziano et al. (1998): preschool teachers' predictions
studies.finding: Teachers' predictions of 3-6-year-olds' adult personalities matched the children's Big Five scores.

studies.title: Heller et al. (2004); Lischetzke & Eid (2006)
studies.finding: Extraversion positively and neuroticism negatively related to emotional well-being.

studies.title: Costa & McCrae (1984); Watson et al. (1992)
studies.finding: People high in extraversion and low in neuroticism are genetically predisposed to emotional stability.

studies.title: Amirkhan, Risinger, & Swickert (1995): coping
studies.finding: Extraverted college students coped better with everyday stress and sought more social support.

studies.title: Schimmack et al. (2004): facets
studies.finding: The depression facet of N and the positive emotions/cheerfulness facet of E were the most consistent predictors of life satisfaction.

studies.title: Bassi et al. (2014); Suldo et al. (2014); Zanon et al. (2014): teenagers
studies.finding: In the US, Brazil and Italy, extraversion related to happiness, optimism and life satisfaction; openness, conscientiousness and low N also involved.

studies.title: McCrae & Costa (1991); Digman (1990); John (1990)
studies.finding: High A and C linked to greater well-being; high A linked to cooperation, helpfulness, altruism, honesty and selflessness.

studies.title: Zhai et al. (2013): Chinese workers
studies.finding: Extraversion, conscientiousness and low neuroticism related to subjective well-being.

studies.title: DeRaad (2000); Jorm (1987); Kotov et al. (2010) and others
studies.finding: High neuroticism associated with psychological distress, depression, anxiety, substance abuse and self-blame.

studies.title: Bluml et al. (2013): suicide in Germany
studies.finding: High N and O linked to greater suicide risk; lowest risk with high E and C.

studies.title: Anderson et al. (2001); Lucas & Diener (2001)
studies.finding: Extraverted students enjoyed higher status; extraverts rated social situations positive only when pleasant.

studies.title: Jensen-Campbell & Malcolm (2007): grades 5-8
studies.finding: Conscientious students were more accepted, had more and better friendships and were less often targets of aggression.

studies.title: Magnus et al. (1993): 4-year college study
studies.finding: Extraverts experienced more positive events; high-N students more negative events (illness, weight gain, tickets, rejection).

studies.title: Mroczek & Almeida (2004): adults 25-74
studies.finding: Everyday stressors had much stronger negative emotional effects for high-neuroticism people.

studies.title: Saudino et al. (1997): Swedish twins
studies.finding: Women high in E and O had more positive life events; women high in N more negative ones.

studies.title: Van der Linden et al. (2010); Meier et al. (2010)
studies.finding: Dutch teens high in E, emotional stability and A judged more popular; Americans high in E and A rated more attractive.

studies.title: McCrae & Costa (1985a, 1985b); Shane et al. (2010) and others
studies.finding: High openness linked to broad interests and career change; O plus E to self-employment; extraverts more active and satisfied in retirement.

studies.title: Back et al. (2006); Conner & Abraham (2001) and others
studies.finding: Conscientious people are reliable, punctual, efficient, get better grades and are more organised and achievement oriented.

studies.title: Poropat (2009); Carver & Connor-Smith (2010); Prinzie et al. (2009)
studies.finding: A, C and O correlated with better college grades, better parenting and better coping with stress.

studies.title: Barrick & Mount (1996); Barrick et al. (1993); Stewart et al. (1996): workplace
studies.finding: Conscientiousness predicted high goals, desirable work behaviour, high ratings and job performance in professional, police, managerial, sales and skilled jobs.

studies.title: Friedman & Martin (2011)
studies.finding: Highly conscientious people tend to be healthier and live longer.

studies.title: Hampson et al. (2000): smokers
studies.finding: More conscientious smokers were less likely to smoke at home.

studies.title: Raynor & Levine (2009): health habits
studies.finding: Conscientious students wore seat belts, exercised, slept enough and ate more fruit and vegetables.

studies.title: Skinner et al. (2002): diabetes
studies.finding: More conscientious young diabetics sought more information and were more diligent about self-care.

studies.title: Ferguson (2000); Tucker, Elliott, & Klein (2006)
studies.finding: Conscientious people had fewer hypochondriacal complaints and took more responsibility for healthy behaviour.

studies.title: Nigg et al. (2002): ADHD
studies.finding: ADHD symptoms were significantly lower in people higher in agreeableness.

studies.title: Christensen et al. (2002): renal insufficiency
studies.finding: Patients higher in neuroticism on the NEO had a 37.5% higher mortality rate over 4 years.

studies.title: Eysenck (2009); Friedman, Kern, & Reynolds (2010); Williams et al. (2010)
studies.finding: High neuroticism predicted poorer health and well-being in old age but greater longevity, and fewer dementia-type cognitive declines.

studies.title: Jokela et al. (2014); Lee et al. (2014): stroke and heart disease
studies.finding: Higher E linked to stroke risk; high C to lower death risk from stroke and heart disease; high N to heart disease.

studies.title: Hintsanen et al. (2014): sleep
studies.finding: High E, A and C linked to more and better sleep; high N to worse sleep.

studies.title: Shim et al. (2014): weight in Korea
studies.finding: Overweight men were high in openness and low in conscientiousness; overweight women low in neuroticism and openness.

studies.title: Walton & Roberts (2004): substance use
studies.finding: Low C and A predicted heavy alcohol or illegal drug use.

studies.title: Livingston et al. (2014): sexual minorities
studies.finding: Those high in E and C showed high levels of drug and alcohol use.

studies.title: Benotsch et al. (2013): prescription drugs
studies.finding: High N and O predicted using prescription drugs not prescribed for oneself.

studies.title: Laursen, Pulkkinen, & Adams (2002): 25-year Finnish study
studies.finding: High agreeableness meant less alcoholism and depression, fewer arrests and greater career stability.

studies.title: O'Riordan & O'Connell (2014): Irish adolescents
studies.finding: Agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism and extraversion were linked to criminal behaviour.

studies.title: Andreassen et al. (2013): Norwegian students
studies.finding: N linked to Internet, exercise and study addiction and compulsive buying; E to Facebook and smartphone addiction, exercise addiction and compulsive buying.

studies.title: Asendorpf & Wilpers (1998): German first-year students
studies.finding: Extraverts made more friends and fell in love more; agreeable students had less opposite-sex conflict; conscientious ones kept family contact; openness had no effect.

studies.title: Jonkmann et al. (2013): living arrangements
studies.finding: Those staying with parents were low in openness; roommates increased openness; romantic partners increased conscientiousness.

studies.title: Barelds (2005): Dutch couples
studies.finding: Low neuroticism and high extraversion in both partners related to marital happiness.

studies.title: Watson & Humrichouse (2006): newlyweds
studies.finding: Self-ratings of A and C rose and N fell over 2 years, but spouses rated declines in C, A, E and O.

studies.title: Roberts & Robins (2000): life goals
studies.finding: Students wanting higher economic, social and political status scored high in E and low in A.

studies.title: Gosling, Sandy, & Potter (2010): dog vs cat people
studies.finding: Dog people scored higher in E, A and C and lower in N and O than cat people.

studies.title: Paunonen (1998); Paunonen & Ashton (2001): factors vs traits
studies.finding: Both factors and lower-level traits predict well, but trait validities were higher.

studies.title: Ashton & Lee (2009): HEXACO inventories
studies.finding: The HEXACO-PI-R and HEXACO-60 are valid and reliable; factors documented in many cultures.

studies.title: Chirumbolo & Leone (2010): Italian voting
studies.finding: High conscientiousness linked to right-wing voting; left-wing voters higher in honesty, agreeableness and openness.

studies.title: Sibley et al. (2010): New Zealand students
studies.finding: Low openness and emotionality linked to right-wing authoritarianism and prejudice toward dissident groups.

studies.title: Johnson, Rowatt, & Petrini (2011): job performance
studies.finding: Employed Americans high in honesty/humility received higher job performance ratings.

studies.title: Aghababaei (2012); Aghababaei & Arji (2014); Oliveira (2013)
studies.finding: Honesty/humility correlated with religious feelings but not happiness (Egypt); it did correlate with happiness among Portuguese students.

studies.title: Dunlop et al. (2012); Rollison et al. (2013): offenders
studies.finding: Delinquents in England and criminals in Australia scored low on honesty/humility and high on psychoticism.

studies.title: Paulhus & Williams (2002): the Dark Triad
studies.finding: Introduced narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy as the darker side of personality.

studies.title: James et al. (2014); Porter et al. (2014)
studies.finding: High Dark Triad scorers engaged in more antisocial activities and enjoyed others' misfortune more.

studies.title: Paulhus & Webster (2010)
studies.finding: Dark Triad scorers showed strong self-promotion and were cold, duplicitous and aggressive.

studies.title: Garcia & Silkstrom (2014): Facebook updates
studies.finding: The verbal content of Facebook updates validly predicted psychopathy and narcissism; posts were cold, aggressive and self-promoting.

studies.title: Giammarco & Vernon (2014); Muris et al. (2013); Oliveira (2013)
studies.finding: High Machiavellianism and psychopathy linked to low C, A and O, low empathy, high aggression, vengefulness and low emotional stability.

studies.title: Adams et al. (2014); Baughman et al. (2014): sexual behaviour
studies.finding: Dark Triad linked to short-term exploitative sexual relationships; psychopathy to high sex drive and sadomasochistic fantasies.

studies.title: Montag, Jurkiewicz, & Reuter (2010): Germany
studies.finding: Internet addiction greater among those high in neuroticism and excessively self-focused.

studies.title: Tosun & Lajunen (2010): Turkey
studies.finding: High psychoticism students used the Internet as a substitute for face-to-face interaction.

studies.title: Amichai-Hamburger & Vinitzky (2010): Israel
studies.finding: High conscientiousness meant more Facebook friends; high neuroticism meant more photos posted.

studies.title: Lonnqvist et al. (2014): Finland
studies.finding: High extraversion scorers had more Facebook friends.

studies.title: Van der Aa et al. (2009): Netherlands
studies.finding: Compulsive Internet use greatest among introverted, disagreeable, emotionally less stable, lonely adolescents.

studies.title: Muller et al. (2014): video game addiction
studies.finding: Highest among those high in N and low in C and E.

studies.title: Karl, Peluchette, & Schlaegel (2010): US and Germany
studies.finding: High C, A and emotional stability students posted less about substance abuse or sex; Americans posted more than Germans regardless of personality.

studies.title: Mark & Ganzach (2014); Correa et al. (2010): social media use
studies.finding: High extraversion adults used social media more; men high in emotional instability even more.

studies.title: Huang & Yang (2010): online shopping in Taiwan
studies.finding: Conscientious students shopped online for convenience, open ones for adventure, neurotic ones to avoid people.

studies.title: Ryan & Xenos (2011): Australia
studies.finding: High E, low C and social loneliness predicted Facebook use.

studies.title: Witt, Massman, & Jackson (2011): ages 11-16
studies.finding: High openness youths spent more time on computers and video games.

studies.title: Delevi & Weisskirch (2013): sexting
studies.finding: Students who sent suggestive photos were high in N and low in A.

studies.title: Brody (1997); Buss (1988); Stelmack (1997): heritability
studies.finding: Inheritance may account for as much as 50% of personality, most strongly for E, N and P.

examples.title: Surface vs source traits: the nervous exam-taker
examples.text: A student fidgets, cannot decide which question to attempt and fears failing even easy papers. An observer might call this 'nervousness', but in Cattell's terms that is a surface trait: a cluster of correlated behaviours. Underneath could lie source traits such as high O (apprehensive) and high Q4 (tense).

examples.title: Environmental-mold traits: hostel vs home
examples.text: Two cousins with similar temperaments grow up apart: one in a strict boarding school, the other in a relaxed joint family. The punctuality and routine of the first are environmental-mold traits, patterns imposed by surroundings rather than biology.

examples.title: Cortical arousal at a wedding
examples.text: At a loud wedding sangeet, one friend is on the dance floor all night while another slips out to a quiet room after an hour. Eysenck would say the first, an extravert, has low base arousal and seeks stimulation, while the second, an introvert, is already highly aroused and finds the noise overwhelming.

examples.title: Conscientiousness in college
examples.text: A student who keeps a study timetable, submits assignments early and never misses a lab fits the Big Five profile of high conscientiousness, which the chapter links to better grades, healthier habits and better job performance later.

examples.title: Dark Triad at work
examples.text: A colleague who flatters the boss, takes credit for others' work and shows no remorse when caught displays Machiavellian and psychopathic tendencies, the kind of items the Dirty Dozen Scale asks about.

checks.q: Cattell's main goal in studying personality was to
options: predict how a person will behave in a given situation
change abnormal behaviour into normal behaviour
uncover unconscious conflicts through case studies
checks.explain: Cattell aimed to predict behaviour in normal people, not to treat or modify it (p. 214).

checks.q: In factor analysis, if two scales correlate highly, Cattell concluded that they
options: measure the same or a related aspect of personality
checks.explain: Highly correlated measures are combined into a single dimension or factor (p. 214).

checks.q: Cattell did his graduate work with the developer of factor analysis,
checks.explain: Spearman developed factor analysis and used it for mental abilities; Cattell applied it to personality (p. 215).

checks.q: Which childhood experience did Cattell link to his serious, work-dedicated outlook?
options: A long period of illness keeping him from school
Seeing trainloads of wounded World War I soldiers
checks.explain: At 9 he saw wounded soldiers arriving at a nearby hospital, making him aware of life's brevity (p. 215).

checks.q: A trait possessed by everyone to some degree, such as intelligence, is a
checks.explain: Common traits are universal, differing only in degree (p. 216).

checks.q: Anxiety, indecision and irrational fear combining into 'neuroticism' illustrates a
checks.explain: Surface traits correlate but have no single source, so are less stable (p. 217).

checks.q: Carelessness and slurred speech caused by alcohol are Cattell's example of
checks.explain: Constitutional traits come from biological conditions but are not necessarily innate (p. 218).

checks.q: The different behaviour of a career military officer and a jazz musician illustrates
checks.explain: Environmental-mold traits are learned from social and physical environments (p. 218).

checks.q: Cattell's 16 source traits are measured by the
checks.explain: The 16 source traits are best known through the 16 PF Questionnaire (p. 218).

checks.q: Cattell compared source traits in personality to
checks.explain: Source traits are the basic elements of personality, as atoms are of the physical world (p. 219).

checks.q: Cattell said a personality theory that ignores dynamic traits is like
options: describing an engine without mentioning its fuel
checks.explain: Dynamic (motivating) traits are the fuel of behaviour (p. 219).

checks.q: Dynamic traits are concerned with
checks.explain: Dynamic traits are the driving forces of behaviour (p. 217).

checks.q: Cattell concluded that overall, the proportion of personality that is genetically based is about
checks.explain: One-third genetic, two-thirds social and environmental (p. 219).

checks.q: According to Cattell's data, about 80 percent of which factors are genetic?
checks.explain: Factors B and H were about 80% genetic (p. 219).

checks.q: Cattell regarded the major formative period of personality as
checks.explain: Infancy is the major formative period, with weaning and toilet training (p. 220).

checks.q: Cattell's late maturity stage is compared in the chapter to
checks.explain: Re-examining values and seeking a new self resembles Jung's midlife (p. 221).

checks.q: On free will vs determinism, Cattell falls more on the side of
checks.explain: Predictability requires lawful, orderly behaviour, leaving little spontaneity (p. 221).

checks.q: Which statement fits Cattell's view of human nature?
options: Psychosexual conflicts push us from the past
Childhood matters but does not permanently determine personality
A drive for self-actualisation pulls us forward
checks.explain: He proposed no ultimate goal and did not see childhood as permanently determining (p. 221).

checks.q: Observer ratings of a person's absences from work and sociability in the office are
checks.explain: L-data are life records of overt behaviour in real settings (p. 222).

checks.q: Why did Cattell call tests like the Rorschach 'objective'?
checks.explain: The person cannot tell what is measured; most psychologists still call them subjective (p. 222).

checks.q: The 16 PF Test is intended for people aged
checks.explain: It is for those 16 and over, though child and adolescent versions exist (p. 223).

checks.q: The sample 16 PF profile of the airline pilot showed the person to be
checks.explain: The pilot was stable, conscientious, adventurous, controlled and relaxed (p. 223).

checks.q: Cattell's P technique involves
options: correlating data from a large group
