practice.q: What is factor analysis? (2 marks)
practice.answer: Factor analysis is a statistical technique that correlates every possible pair of measures taken from a group of people to find underlying common factors. When two measures correlate highly (for example, anxiety and introversion scales), they are taken to tap the same characteristic and are combined into one factor. Cattell called these factors traits.

practice.q: Distinguish constitutional traits from environmental-mold traits. (2 marks)
practice.answer: Both are types of source traits classified by origin. Constitutional traits arise from biological or physiological conditions, though not necessarily innate (e.g. carelessness and slurred speech after drinking alcohol). Environmental-mold traits are learned from social and physical surroundings (e.g. differences between someone raised in poverty and someone raised in luxury, or a military officer and a jazz musician).

practice.q: According to Cattell's research, which source traits are determined primarily by heredity? (2 marks)
practice.answer: From 16 PF data on 3,000 males aged 12 to 18, Cattell (1982) found Factor F (serious vs happy-go-lucky), Factor I (tough- vs tender-minded) and Factor Q3 (uncontrolled vs controlled) to be mainly hereditary, while E, G and Q4 were mainly environmental. Earlier twin and sibling comparisons also showed about 80% of intelligence (B) and boldness (H) to be genetic.

practice.q: Which Freudian ideas did Cattell incorporate into his stages of development? (2 marks)
practice.answer: Although not a follower of Freud, Cattell accepted two Freudian ideas in his infancy stage (birth to 6): that the early years of life are crucial for forming personality, and that oral and anal conflicts (linked to weaning and toilet training) can affect personality. Ego, superego and social attitudes also form in this stage.

practice.q: What is self-sentiment, and what is its role in personality? (2 marks) [Review Question 8]
practice.answer: This edition of the chapter does not define self-sentiment. What it does say is that dynamic traits are the motivating forces of behaviour, covering our motivations, interests and ambitions, and that Cattell thought a theory without them is like an engine described without its fuel. For a full answer on self-sentiment, consult a fuller text on Cattell's dynamic traits.

practice.q: Distinguish Cattell's R technique from his P technique. (2 marks)
practice.answer: Both are forms of factor analysis in Cattell's multivariate approach. The R technique collects large amounts of data from a group of people and correlates all the scores to identify traits. The P technique collects a large amount of data from a single subject over a long period of time.

practice.q: Describe the behaviour of people who score high in psychoticism on Eysenck's test. (2 marks)
practice.answer: High psychoticism scorers are aggressive, antisocial, tough-minded, cold and egocentric, and can be cruel, hostile and insensitive to others. They have low emotional well-being and more problems with alcohol, drugs and violent crime, yet can be highly creative. Men score higher, possibly due to male hormones.

practice.q: Name the three Dark Triad traits. (2 marks)
practice.answer: Paulhus and Williams (2002) proposed narcissism (extreme selfishness, inflated self-view, need for admiration), Machiavellianism (manipulating others through cunning and deceit) and psychopathy (callous, egocentric, antisocial exploitation of others using charm and often violence). They are quickly measured by the 12-item Dirty Dozen Scale.

practice.q: How does Cattell's concept of traits differ from Allport's? Answer from what the chapter says about Cattell. (5 marks) [Review Question 1]
practice.answer:
The chapter does not set out Allport's trait theory itself, so the answer rests on what is distinctive about Cattell's traits.

Derived statistically. For Cattell, traits are factors derived by factor analysis of large amounts of data from normal people, often more than 50 measures per subject. A trait is whatever cluster of highly correlated measures emerges from the statistics, not a category arrived at by intuition or case study. Cattell defined traits as relatively permanent reaction tendencies, the basic structural units or mental elements of personality.

Purpose: prediction. Cattell's traits exist to predict behaviour; he defined personality as that which permits prediction of what a person will do in a given situation.

Elaborate classification. Cattell classified traits several ways: common vs unique (shared by all vs few), ability vs temperament vs dynamic (efficiency, emotional style, motivation), surface vs source (correlated clusters vs stable unitary factors) and, for source traits, constitutional vs environmental-mold (biological vs learned origin). The 16 source traits are measured by the 16 PF.

Common ground. The chapter does note that Allport was Cattell's colleague at Harvard, and that Allport and Cattell were among the first to argue that inherited factors shape personality and rank in importance with environment. Both also recognised traits that are common to people and traits that are individual or unique.

practice.q: Explain how traits can be identified through factor analysis. (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Factor analysis, developed by Spearman and applied by Cattell to personality, is the method by which Cattell identified traits.

Procedure. Many measures (test scores, subscales, ratings) are collected from a group, often over 50 per subject. The correlation between every possible pair of measures is computed. When two measures correlate highly, they are taken to tap the same or a related aspect of personality; for example, highly correlated anxiety and introversion scales would be treated as measuring one characteristic. These measures are combined into a single dimension or factor, which Cattell called a trait. Repeating this across all measures yields the basic factors; after more than two decades, Cattell identified 16 source traits.

Forms. In the R technique, large amounts of data from a group are correlated; in the P technique, many measures are gathered from one person over a long period.

Limitations. Critics note that subjectivity can enter when choosing tests and behaviours to measure, choosing the factor-analytic technique and the significance level, and labelling the factors. This may explain why others struggled to replicate Cattell's 16 traits, and why Eysenck supplemented factor analysis with experiments. Different measurement choices also explain why Cattell found 16 factors, Eysenck 3 and McCrae and Costa 5.

practice.q: Describe three ways of categorising traits according to Cattell, and define surface and source traits with examples. (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Cattell saw traits as relatively permanent reaction tendencies and classified them in three main ways.

1. Common vs unique traits. Common traits (intelligence, extraversion, gregariousness) are possessed by everyone in varying degrees, because people share similar heredity and social pressures. Unique traits belong to one or few people and show in interests and attitudes, such as a passion for genealogy or Chinese martial arts.

2. Ability, temperament and dynamic traits. Ability traits govern how efficiently we pursue goals (intelligence). Temperament traits describe the emotional style of behaviour (assertive, easygoing, irritable). Dynamic traits are motivating forces: our interests and ambitions.

3. Surface vs source traits. Surface traits are characteristics that correlate but do not form a factor because they have no single source; anxiety, indecision and irrational fear combine into the surface trait of neuroticism. They are less stable and can vary with situations. Source traits are unitary, stable, permanent factors that combine to produce surface traits; examples are the 16 PF factors, such as A (reserved vs outgoing) or H (timid vs bold).

Source traits are further divided by origin into constitutional traits (biological, e.g. behaviour from alcohol) and environmental-mold traits (learned from surroundings).

practice.q: How does Cattell's image of human nature differ from Freud's? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Cattell's view follows from his definition of personality as what permits prediction of behaviour.

Determinism. Like Freud, Cattell leaned toward determinism; predictability requires lawful, orderly behaviour and leaves little room for spontaneity. But his determinism is statistical and trait-based, not driven by unconscious instincts.

No psychosexual push. Cattell proposed no ultimate goal dominating behaviour: no drive toward self-actualisation and, unlike Freud, no psychosexual conflicts pushing us from the past.

Childhood. Cattell accepted that early life matters and borrowed Freud's ideas that the early years are crucial and that oral and anal conflicts can affect personality. But, unlike Freud, he did not think childhood forces determine personality permanently; his stages run through maturity, late maturity and old age, with personality continuing to change.

Nature and nurture. Cattell explicitly weighted both, estimating one-third of personality as genetic and two-thirds environmental, through constitutional and environmental-mold traits.

Uniqueness. He took a moderate position, recognising both common and unique traits.

Optimism. He began optimistic about solving social problems but came to believe human nature and society had regressed.

Method. His subjects were normal people studied by factor analysis, whereas Freud built his view from disturbed patients; Cattell called clinicians warm-hearted but fuzzy-headed.

practice.q: Identify the three types of data Cattell collected and give an example of each. (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Cattell used three primary objective assessment techniques.

L-data (life records). Observers rate specific overt behaviours in natural, real-life settings rather than a laboratory. Examples: frequency of absence from work, school grades, conscientiousness in job duties, emotional stability on the soccer field, sociability in the office.

Q-data (questionnaires). People rate themselves on questionnaires, inventories and attitude scales; the 16 PF is the best-known example. Cattell warned of two limitations: some people have only superficial self-awareness, and others may deliberately falsify answers. So Q-data must not be assumed accurate; research later confirmed the 16 PF can be faked (Simon, 2007).

T-data (tests). 'Objective' tests in which the person cannot tell what is being measured, so cannot distort answers. Examples: Rorschach inkblots, the Thematic Apperception Test and the word-association test. Shown an inkblot, you cannot predict whether your answer will reveal you as conservative or apprehensive.

Evaluation. Most psychologists find calling these tests objective misleading, since scoring and interpretation are open to bias; Cattell meant only that they resist faking. Using three kinds of data lets weaknesses of one source be offset by another.

practice.q: How do people high in extraversion on Eysenck's test differ from those who score low? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Description. High scorers on the E dimension are extraverts: oriented to the outside world, preferring others' company, sociable, lively, active, impulsive, adventurous, assertive, dominant, sensation seeking, carefree and venturesome. Low scorers are introverts.

Emotions and performance. High E scorers experience more pleasant emotions and are happier (Fisher & Francis, 2013; Lucas & Fujita, 2000). Extraverted businessmen performed difficult tasks better than introverted ones (Campbell et al., 2011). Increasing work and social satisfaction went with higher E (Scollon & Diener, 2006).

Biology. Eysenck found extraverts have a lower base level of cortical arousal. Hence they need and seek excitement and stimulation, while introverts, already highly aroused, avoid it.

Sensory sensitivity. Introverts react more strongly to sensory stimulation, show greater sensitivity to low-level stimuli and have lower pain thresholds. Later research supports these differences but finds less convincing evidence that they come from cortical arousal.

Stability and heredity. Introverted children tend to stay introverted into adulthood (Ganiban et al., 2008), and the differences are genetically based, with E among the dimensions most strongly inherited.

practice.q: How does Eysenck's research on identical and fraternal twins and on adopted children support his view of genetic factors? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Eysenck's position. He held that traits and dimensions are primarily inherited, with environment (such as childhood family interactions) having only limited effects. Genetic evidence is stronger for extraversion and neuroticism than for psychoticism.

Twin studies. Identical (monozygotic) twins share all their genes; fraternal (dizygotic) twins do not. Eysenck found identical twins more alike in personality than fraternal twins, even when the identical twins were raised by different parents in different environments. If upbringing were decisive, twins raised apart should differ; their similarity points to heredity.

Adoption studies. Adopted children's personalities resemble their biological parents more than their adoptive parents, even when they never had contact with their biological parents. Since the adoptive parents provided the environment, this again supports heredity.

Cross-cultural support. The same three dimensions appear in more than 35 nations including the US, England, Japan, China, Nigeria and Sweden, which the chapter takes as further evidence that inherited factors are primary.

Qualification. Some environment still matters: high psychoticism scorers had more authoritarian parents (Heaven & Ciarrochi, 2006).

practice.q: How do people high in extraversion and in conscientiousness differ from low scorers? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Extraversion. High scorers have greater emotional well-being and life satisfaction, cope better with everyday stress and seek social support (Amirkhan et al., 1995), enjoy higher status among peers (Anderson et al., 2001) and experience more positive events like good grades and pay rises (Magnus et al., 1993). They make more friends and fall in love more often (Asendorpf & Wilpers, 1998), are more active and satisfied in retirement, are more likely self-employed when also open, and are rated more attractive when also agreeable. Drawbacks: higher stroke risk, and links to Facebook and smartphone addiction and compulsive buying.

Conscientiousness. High scorers are reliable, responsible, punctual, efficient and dependable and earn better grades; they are organised, self-disciplined and achievement oriented (Conner & Abraham, 2001). At work they set high goals and receive high ratings; conscientiousness predicts job performance in professional, police, managerial, sales and skilled jobs (Barrick & Mount, 1996). They are healthier and live longer (Friedman & Martin, 2011), wear seat belts, exercise, sleep well and eat more fruit and vegetables, manage diabetes diligently, report fewer hypochondriacal complaints and have lower death risk from stroke and heart disease. Conscientious children are more accepted by peers, and conscientious students keep closer family contact. Low scorers are more likely to be heavy drinkers or drug users.

practice.q: What are the emotional and behavioural correlates of high scores in neuroticism? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Emotional correlates. Neuroticism is negatively related to well-being. High scorers show psychological distress and proneness to depression, anxiety, substance abuse and self-blame (Kotov et al., 2010). Everyday stressors hit them harder (Mroczek & Almeida, 2004) and they experience more negative events such as illness, weight gain and rejections (Magnus et al., 1993). With high openness they show greater suicide risk (Bluml et al., 2013). Eysenck traced this to an overreactive sympathetic nervous system.

Cognitive and work. Lower verbal abilities and more cognitive impairment 25 years later (Crowe et al., 2006), yet better performance in fast-paced, stressful jobs (Smillie et al., 2006).

Health. Renal patients high in N had 37.5% higher mortality; N predicts heart disease and poor sleep; yet it was also linked to greater longevity and fewer dementia-type declines, so neurotics may live longer but unhappily.

Addictive and online behaviour. Internet, exercise and study addiction and compulsive buying (Andreassen et al., 2013), video-game addiction, misuse of others' prescription drugs, posting more photos on Facebook, shopping online to avoid people, and sexting. With psychoticism, high N correlates with crime (Huo-Liang, 2006).

Relationships. Low N in both partners predicts marital happiness.

practice.q: What are the dimensions of the HEXACO model and how do they differ from the five-factor model? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Michael Ashton and Kibeom Lee proposed HEXACO (2007, 2009), an acronym from its six factors.

The six factors. Honesty/humility (sincere, honest, faithful vs greedy, pretentious, hypocritical, boastful); Emotionality (emotional, oversensitive, anxious vs brave, tough, stable); Extraversion (outgoing, lively, sociable vs shy, withdrawn); Agreeableness (tolerant, peaceful, gentle vs quarrelsome, stubborn, ill-tempered); Conscientiousness (disciplined, diligent, precise vs reckless, lazy, irresponsible); Openness to experience (creative, unconventional vs shallow, conventional).

Differences from the Big Five. Six factors instead of five. Only extraversion and conscientiousness are similar to the five-factor model; the other four differ to varying degrees and are unique to HEXACO. The main addition is honesty/humility, and emotionality takes the place of neuroticism.

Assessment and support. The 100-item HEXACO-PI-R and the 60-item HEXACO-60 are valid and reliable, and the factors appear in over a dozen cultures.

Correlates. Honesty/humility predicts higher job ratings and stronger religious feeling and is low in offenders (with high psychoticism); conscientiousness predicts right-wing voting in Italy; low openness and emotionality predict authoritarianism and prejudice.

practice.q: What traits constitute the Dark Triad, and how can they affect behaviour? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams (2002) proposed the Dark Triad to capture the darker side of personality.

The traits. Narcissism: extreme selfishness, inflated sense of one's abilities and constant need for admiration and attention. Machiavellianism: manipulating others through cunning, deceit and unscrupulous behaviour. Psychopathy: callous, insensitive, egocentric and antisocial exploitation of others with charm and often violence.

Assessment. The 12-item Dirty Dozen Scale (Jonason & Webster, 2010) asks about manipulation, lying, flattery, exploitation, lack of remorse, cynicism, and wanting admiration, attention, status and special favours.

Effects on behaviour. High scorers engage in more antisocial activity and enjoy others' misfortune; they self-promote strongly and are cold, duplicitous and aggressive. Their Facebook updates are cold, aggressive and self-promoting, and can predict psychopathy and narcissism. High Machiavellianism and psychopathy go with low conscientiousness, agreeableness and openness, little empathy, vengefulness and low emotional stability. Sexually, the Triad is linked to short-term exploitative relationships; psychopathy to high sex drive with sadomasochistic fantasies.

Conclusion. The traits can lead to antisocial, duplicitous and aggressive behaviour.

practice.q: In what ways do personality traits influence online behaviour? (5 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. The Internet both reflects and influences personality, and the chapter's traits predict how people use it.

Eysenck's dimensions. German students high in neuroticism and self-focus were more prone to Internet addiction; Turkish students high in psychoticism used the Internet as a substitute for face-to-face contact.

Five-factor findings. Extraversion: more Facebook friends (Finland), more social media use (US), and, with low conscientiousness and loneliness, more Facebook use (Australia). Conscientiousness: more Facebook friends (Israel), less posting about substance abuse or sex, shopping online for convenience. Neuroticism: more photo posting, Internet and gaming addiction, shopping online to avoid people, sexting (with low agreeableness); emotionally unstable US men used social sites even more. Openness: shopping online for adventure, more computer and video game time among 11-16-year-olds. Compulsive use in Dutch adolescents was greatest among introverted, disagreeable, less stable, lonely teens.

Culture. Americans posted more personal content than Germans regardless of traits.

Personal application. A student could reflect, for example, on whether they use social media to connect (extraversion) or to avoid people (neuroticism).

practice.q: Describe Eysenck's three dimensions of personality. Are they determined mainly by genetic or environmental factors? (10 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Hans Eysenck, working at London's Maudsley Hospital and Institute of Psychiatry, agreed with Cattell that personality consists of traits derived by factor analysis, but criticised the technique's subjectivity and Cattell's poor replicability. He therefore combined factor analysis with personality tests and experiments. With his wife Sybil he developed the Eysenck Personality Inventory (12 years, 20 factor analyses), now used in nearly 40 countries. His theory reduces personality to three dimensions, or superfactors.

Extraversion vs introversion (E). Extraverts are sociable, lively, active, assertive, sensation seeking, carefree, dominant and venturesome; introverts are the opposite pole. Extraverts experience more pleasant emotions and happiness, and extraverted businessmen handle difficult tasks better. Eysenck found extraverts have a lower base level of cortical arousal, so they seek stimulation; introverts, already highly aroused, avoid it, are more sensitive to low-level stimuli and have lower pain thresholds. The behavioural differences are well supported, though the arousal explanation less so.

Neuroticism vs emotional stability (N). Neurotics are anxious, depressed, guilt-prone, low in self-esteem, tense, irrational, shy and moody. Eysenck held that in neurotics the sympathetic nervous system overreacts even to mild stress, causing chronic hypersensitivity and emotional reactions to trivial events. Research shows neurotics may excel in fast-paced stressful jobs but score lower in verbal ability and show more cognitive impairment later in life; rising work and social satisfaction goes with lower N.

Psychoticism vs impulse control (P). High scorers are aggressive, cold, egocentric, impersonal, impulsive, antisocial, tough-minded, cruel and insensitive, with more alcohol, drug and violent crime problems, yet can be very creative. Men score higher, which Eysenck linked to male hormones. Criminal behaviour correlates with high P and N (Huo-Liang, 2006). Eysenck believed society needs all these types; a high-P person might become disturbed or criminal, or channel aggression into acceptable work like coaching football.

Stability. The dimensions are stable through life, especially E and N; introverted children remain introverted adults.

Genes or environment? Eysenck concluded the dimensions are determined primarily by heredity, more strongly for E and N than P. Environmental influences such as family interactions are not ruled out but are limited. Evidence: (1) identical twins are more alike than fraternal twins even when reared apart; (2) adopted children resemble biological more than adoptive parents, even without contact; (3) the same three dimensions appear in over 35 nations, from the US and England to China, Japan and Nigeria; (4) the neuroticism reactivity is described as innate. He also estimated intelligence, which shapes personality complexity, at 80% inherited.

Qualifications. Environment still plays some role: high-P scorers had more authoritarian, controlling parents. Later researchers felt three dimensions were too few, leading to the five-factor model, whose extraversion and neuroticism match Eysenck's and whose agreeableness and conscientiousness resemble low psychoticism.

Conclusion. Eysenck offered a parsimonious, biologically grounded model, supported by twin, adoption and cross-cultural data, which established heredity as a primary influence on personality while leaving a limited role for environment.

practice.q: Describe McCrae and Costa's five factors of personality. Discuss the role of heredity and environment, cross-cultural findings and stability over time. (10 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Researchers felt Eysenck's three dimensions were too few and Cattell's sixteen too many. From the 1980s, Robert McCrae and Paul Costa at the NIH Gerontology Research Center in Baltimore identified five robust factors, the Big Five, which McCrae (2011) called a turning point in personality psychology.

The five factors. Neuroticism: worried, insecure, nervous, highly strung. Extraversion: sociable, talkative, fun-loving, affectionate. Openness: original, independent, creative, daring. Agreeableness: good-natured, softhearted, trusting, courteous. Conscientiousness: careful, reliable, hardworking, organised.

Measurement. The factors were confirmed by self-ratings, objective tests and observer reports. The NEO Personality Inventory (from N, E, O) remains the most used measure, with an Internet short form and quicker 100- and 40-adjective checklists. Like all self-reports, it can be faked.

Heredity vs environment. Twin studies show N, E, O and C have a stronger hereditary component, while agreeableness has a stronger environmental component (Bergeman et al., 1993; Pedersen et al., 1988). E and N resemble Eysenck's inherited dimensions; A and C may be the low end of his psychoticism; openness correlates with intelligence; agreeableness with Adler's social interest.

Cross-cultural findings. The factors appear in more than 50 nations, Eastern and Western, suggesting a common human structure of personality and supporting a genetic basis. But they were not found in an isolated, largely illiterate Bolivian tribe, and the studied countries tend to be urban and educated. Cultures value factors differently: Japan prizes conscientiousness, Hong Kong and India agreeableness, Singapore emotional stability, Venezuela extraversion, Australia extraversion and agreeableness. Europeans and Americans score higher in E and O and lower in A than Asians and Africans. Women in 55 countries report higher N, E, A and C than men, especially in prosperous, egalitarian nations. People see themselves as more neurotic and open, and others as more conscientious.

Stability over time. All five showed high stability over 6 years (Costa & McCrae, 1988); E and N were stable across a 40-year age span in Finnish twins; extraverted students remained extraverted 20 years later; E and C were most stable over 40 years. Yet there are maturational changes: openness rose in adolescence; from adolescence to adulthood N, E and O declined while A and C rose; and a review found N, E and O decrease and A and C increase by the 60s (Debast et al., 2014). Preschool teachers accurately predicted children's adult Big Five scores, raising the possibility that adults reinforce inherited tendencies.

Predictive value. The factors predict well-being, success, health, addiction, crime, relationships and online behaviour; conscientiousness predicts grades, job performance and longevity, while neuroticism predicts distress. Narrow traits predict even better than broad factors.

Conclusion. The model is well replicated, biologically based and broadly universal among literate societies, though agreeableness shows environmental influence and not all psychologists accept five as the final number, as HEXACO shows.

practice.q: Critically evaluate Cattell's trait theory of personality. (10 marks)
practice.answer:
Introduction. Raymond Cattell, trained under Spearman, applied factor analysis to normal people's personality. His aim was prediction: personality is what permits prediction of behaviour in a given situation.

Core concepts. Traits are relatively permanent reaction tendencies, the basic structural units of personality. He classified them as common vs unique; ability, temperament and dynamic; and surface vs source, with source traits split into constitutional (biological) and environmental-mold (learned). Over two decades of factor analysis yielded 16 source traits (A to Q4), measured by the 16 PF, and later temperament traits like zest and politeness. Dynamic traits supply motivation, the fuel of the engine.

Heredity, development and human nature. Twin and sibling comparisons suggested about one-third of personality is genetic (80% for B and H). He described six stages from infancy to old age, borrowing Freud's emphasis on early years and oral and anal conflicts while extending development across life. He leaned toward determinism, rejected any ultimate goal, accepted both nature and nurture and took a middle position on uniqueness.

Assessment and research. He used L-data (observer ratings in real life), Q-data (self-reports, open to poor insight and faking) and T-data (fake-resistant tests). He rejected bivariate experiments as too narrow and clinical methods as too subjective, preferring multivariate R and P techniques.

Strengths.
1. Rigorous, empirical and comprehensive; Horn judged it unrivalled in adherence to evidence.
2. The 16 PF is widely used for research, diagnosis and job selection, in about 40 languages, with special versions.
3. Research support: the 16 PF predicts marital stability; some traits (F, I, Q3) mainly hereditary and others (E, G, Q4) mainly environmental; valid Greek and Turkish versions.
4. Pioneered behavioral genetics in personality and the trait approach; regarded as the father of trait psychology and one of the 20th century's most influential psychologists.
5. Life-span stages and recognition of person-situation interaction.

Weaknesses.
1. Subjectivity in factor analysis: choosing tests, behaviours, techniques, significance levels and labels.
2. Difficulty replicating his 16 source traits; Eysenck criticised this, and others found 16 too many.
3. The 16 PF can be faked (Simon, 2007) and cannot always be translated (Tshivenda).
4. Calling projective tests objective is misleading to most psychologists.
5. His work is highly technical and remained isolated from mainstream theory; Cattell himself lamented this.

Comparison with later theorists. Eysenck accepted Cattell's factor-analytic starting point but supplemented it with experiments because of the subjectivity problem, and arrived at only three superfactors; later researchers felt Cattell's sixteen factors were too many and Eysenck's three too few, which led McCrae and Costa to five. Cattell's estimate that one-third of personality is inherited is also lower than the chapter's closing estimate of up to 50 percent. In this sense Cattell opened the questions that the rest of the genetics approach tried to answer.

Conclusion. Despite methodological criticisms, Cattell's empirical rigour, his test and his early attention to genetic influence laid foundations that Eysenck, McCrae and Costa and others built upon, so his overall contribution is widely affirmed.

summary: Cattell aimed to predict the behaviour of normal people, using factor analysis to find traits, the basic structural units of personality.
He classified traits as common or unique; ability, temperament or dynamic; and surface or source, with source traits being constitutional (biological) or environmental-mold (learned).
Cattell identified 16 source traits, measured by the 16 PF Test, which is used for research, clinical diagnosis and job selection in about 40 languages.

Twin and sibling comparisons led Cattell to estimate that one-third of personality is genetic; factors B and H are about 80% inherited, and F, I and Q3 are mainly hereditary while E, G and Q4 are mainly environmental.
Cattell proposed six life-span stages (infancy to old age), borrowing Freud's emphasis on the early years and oral and anal conflicts.
Cattell leaned toward determinism, proposed no ultimate goal, accepted both nature and nurture, and took a moderate view on uniqueness.
He assessed personality through L-data, Q-data and T-data and favoured the multivariate approach (R and P techniques) over bivariate and clinical methods.
Factor analysis is criticised for subjectivity and poor replication, but Cattell is seen as the father of the trait approach.
Behavioral genetics studies the link between heredity and personality; Allport and Cattell were early proponents.
Eysenck proposed three largely inherited superfactors: extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism, explained by cortical arousal and sympathetic-nervous-system reactivity.
Twin, adoption and cross-cultural (35+ nations) studies support Eysenck's view that heredity is primary, more for E and N than P.
McCrae and Costa's five-factor model (N, E, O, A, C), measured by the NEO-PI, appears in 50+ nations; four factors are mainly hereditary, agreeableness more environmental.
The Big Five are fairly stable over the life span, with N, E and O declining and A and C rising with age; women report higher N, E, A and C.
The Big Five predict well-being, popularity, grades, job performance, health, addiction, crime, relationships and online behaviour, with conscientiousness especially powerful.
HEXACO (Ashton and Lee) adds honesty/humility and is measured by the HEXACO-PI-R and HEXACO-60.
The Dark Triad (narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy) predicts antisocial, duplicitous, aggressive and sexually exploitative behaviour; it is measured by the Dirty Dozen.
Inheritance may account for up to 50% of personality, but environmental influences cannot be discounted.
